subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
That this House condemn the government for voluntarily relinquishing political sovereignty in the "trade" deal with the United States, namely by limiting the power to decide on new or expanded social programs and cultural industries, including those by the federal, provincial, territorial or municipal governments, present and future.
She said: Madam Speaker, I rise on this Opposition Day to deal with the loss of political sovereignty in the trade deal. This is not a free trade deal which has been negotiated with the United States. It does not save us from countervailing duties being applied by the Americans. It is not free trade under GATT. It pursues a deviation allowed by GATT for two countries to come together when they want to achieve an economic union. We know there is a political price to pay for economic union because institutions have to be changed. It is called harmonization, and that means a loss of our distinctiveness as a country in favour of adopting American institutions, and increasing influence by the American market.
What this is really all about is constitutional change. This deal will bind future Governments. The federal Government is saying it has the power to negotiate an international treaty, but while it is doing so it will bind the provinces, the municipalities and even Indian bands. Indian self-government will be affected. The Territories lose as well. They all lose the power to make economic decisions, create jobs, and pursue social programs unhindered by external considerations such as the trade deal.
Women understand this very much better than men do, it seems. Prominent in the struggle against the trade deal are women's organizations. Right now we have the National Action Committee on the Status of Women in a lobby session
with parliamentarians. They have focused on the trade deal because women are going to be prominent among the economic losers. They also care a great deal about our social programs and institutions such as public broadcasting. They see the need to continue to have the power to design institutions to suit Canada's needs.
Women are not so ideological. They are not in pursuit of the buck. They are prepared to use the public sector, the Government, political power. Women are increasingly entering the mainstream of political life and they do not want to come in and find that their votes do not mean very much because the decisions are going to be made in the U.S. by market forces instead of citizens as voters and parliamentarians.
The Americans understood this aspect of the trade deal very well. They welcomed, for example, the section expanding control over services. They say the agreement establishes the very first international understanding of a comprehensive nature over the service industries under which each side will provide treatment to each other's citizens that is no less favourable than that granted to its own citizens with respect to all new measures affecting services. The agreement provides the right of establishment, the right to cross border sales, and disciplines on public monopolies.
What does that mean? It means whipping them into shape, keeping down the public sector, providing more space for markets and profits. They welcome that. This reference to discipline on public monopolies never appeared on the Canadian side of the elements of the agreement. Why not? Because the Canadian Government is a little bit embarrassed about giving away power, acceding to pressure from the Americans to put this in the trade agreement.
How will the exercise of power be affected by this trade deal? First, if a province wants to start a new social program or expand an existing one or start something like car insurance or a cultural program, it will first have to consider whether it will constitute an unfair subsidy. We do not know the answer to that question in many respects because unfair subsidies remain to be decided upon. We also know that covered services are going to be expanded. We have a list of certain services covered already but more are going to be included as negotiations proceed.
The provinces will also have to consider whether or not whatever it is they want to do infringes on the monopoly section. That refers to covered services which may expand in scope. They will have to look at Section 210 and Section 211 of the trade deal. If what they want to do constitutes a monopoly under the deal, they would have to ask the federal Government to in effect to negotiate on their behalf. The trade deal requires that the provincial, territorial and municipal Governments, as well as Indian bands, ask the federal Government to notify the U.S. Government of an intention to establish a so-called monopoly. In the meantime, the U.S. could retaliate against Canada in some other sector to get equivalent commercial
May 16, 1988

value for the anticipated benefits it might not get if the so-called monopoly went through.
What if the provincial Government concerned is a more progressive Government than the federal Government and wants to do certain things? Perhaps the federal Government will not have a veto, we do not yet know what is in the legislation, but the provincial or territorial Government might not have a great deal of confidence that its interests will be well looked after by the federal Government.
If the matter goes to dispute settlement a panel will be set up. Who is on the panel? At least two Americans, at least two Canadians, and a fifth person to be decided upon by the other four. If they fail to decide, the fifth person would be chosen by lot from a list of potential panel members. These panel members are supposed to be objective. I wonder how objective they can be. Are they going to ignore totally the interests of their country or region? What if there is a conflict? What if the federal Government puts on its list of potential experts only those with the privatization ideology? What if they do not really represent the point of view of the provinces, territories or municipalities which might want to do something a little bit different? We do not know.
I was in a briefing session recently and asked trade officials about car insurance. We have four provinces with public car insurance services. Right now insurance of all kinds is a covered service in the trade agreement. The officials told us they did not know if car insurance would be affected by the trade deal. We would just have to trust them and wait and see. I do not think this is good enough.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: That is not true. That is nonsense.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
I was at the briefing and certainly it was stated that we would not know if car insurance would be included as a covered service. I suspect it would be.
Child care is not covered right now. Fortunately it looks safe. It would not be a monopoly in any event, but what about the management of this service? The management of health care and all kinds of other services comes under the trade deal and that means American corporations have to be treated the same as Canadians in working in what we have normally treated as public sector areas.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Our rules.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: It will not be we who decide. That is what is crucial.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: It certainly will.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: It means we will not have the power to undo decisions made by a previous Government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Nonsense.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
We have some give and take. For example, FIRA was brought in by a Liberal Government to allow review
Supply
of foreign investment for a particular purpose to see what good it would do Canada. The Conservative Government had a mandate and changed that as it was entitled to do. It got rid of FIRA. However, under this trade deal we will not be able to make these kinds of changes. Investment policy will be right in the trade deal and the threshold goes up with respect to the kind of decisions that can be reviewed. If another Government comes in and wants to change it back, which is normal in our political process, it will not have that power. That power will be traded away in the trade deal. It is a weakening of the power of people to use the political process. That is being given away in one fell swoop. These things will be incapable of correction. This weakens the political process.
Women are especially concerned about health care. Large numbers of women work in this industry. Women, of course, are major consumers and they are the health care organizers for their families. This deal looks toward increasing Americanization of our health care services. We have achieved a very high standard of non-profit, publicly organized health care. We are proud of our system. It has been called the best health care system in the world.
The American system excludes coverage of many people. It provides excellent services to some people, those who can afford to pay for highly specialized services, but it is a twotiered system. If we allow our institutions to be changed in that direction we will move toward having a two-tier system with costly services available to some and high quality care not available to all.
We have chosen a different route, the not-for-profit route. Our system is so efficient that there are complaints that it constitutes an unfair subsidy because employers in Canada can rely on our health care system to provide benefits. American employers have to bring in private plans which allow for a profit. They cost a great deal more money and are inefficient. They consider our system such a benefit that it can constitute an unfair subsidy.
According to our Constitution, health care is supposed to be entirely a provincial matter. We have joint programs, but the jurisdiction is provincial. However, under the trade deal aspects of health care get bargained away. The management of all technical services related to the health care system has to be open to American corporations. That is interference with something which should be under provincial jurisdiction.
Our hands will be tied in a very special way in culture despite all the promises that culture was not on the bargaining table. Section 2005 of the trade deal contains a very special notwithstanding clause which is a very important loophole in the deal. It reads:
2. Notwithstanding any other provision of this Agreement, a Party may take measures of equivalent commercial effect in response to actions that would have been inconsistent with this Agreement but for paragraph 1.

May 16, 1988
Supply
Paragraph 1 otherwise exempts culture. Again, it is an exemption with exemptions from the trade deal. It is a clause notwithstanding any other measure in that agreement.
It has been said, and I think correctly, that the trade deal says that we can do whatever we want in culture, with some exceptions, but the Americans can do anything they want in retaliation. This is a very considerable loophole for us.
Further, the Americans realize this and they welcomed it. I will read from the text of the summary of the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement put out by the United States Embassy- right from the horse's mouth. It says:
The U.S. recognizes the importance to Canada of maintaining its cultural identity. At the same time however, the U.S. wants to ensure that Canadian cultural policies do not constitute a discriminatory and unnecessary barrier to U.S. trade.
In other words, whenever they can make a buck they want to be able to make it and not be impeded by our so-called exempting culture. I quote further:
Recognizing Canadian sensitivities, the U.S. has agreed that certain cultural areas are not subject to the specific provisions of the agreement.
Certain are not, but it is very clear that certain are. It continues:
However, the U.S. retains the right to redress any adverse commercial effects of any future cultural measures enacted by Canada.
In addition, Canada has agreed to alter some other things. It says, therefore, that we are on warning that they can retaliate if we take any measures in the future to improve our distinctive Canadian cultural identity.
For example, film distribution is a cultural industry. Is it covered in this agreement? Suppose we wanted to have a policy of Canadian ownership in film distribution, as we have in broadcasting, as was recommended by a task force established by the Government. The current Government does not want to pursue this, but if a future Government wanted to pursue it, the United States could retaliate on behalf of the film distribution interests in the United States. They could use Section 2005 2 against us.
We do not know how many other things they may want to use against us. What about the All News Channel? Would that be against the trade deal? What about newspaper ownership? Suppose we had the threat of a major take-over of our newspapers and wanted to have Canadian ownership. Would our hands be tied in the future? Would we have the possibility of limiting foreign ownership in the cultural sector? It is not at all clear that we could this without retaliation because Section 2005 allows for retaliation.

Madam Speaker, with Meech Lake, Quebec will again become a member of Canada's constitutional family, but what good will that do? Because of the changes imposed by the free trade agreement, the Constitution will have lost much of its
strength. Both federal and provincial powers will be diminished. The provisions of the free trade agreement are in fact so many major amendments to the Canadian Constitution, amendments that cannot be changed later on because there is no formula for amending the free trade agreement. With this so-called international trade treaty, the federal Government is about to weaken the political powers of our federal, provincial, territorial and municipal governments.
Understandably, there is a mass movement of protest against this agreement. The unions, churches, environmentalists, women and Quebec's united stand against free trade are to be commended.
Quebec has used government measures to promote its social programs, investment, performance standards, culture and the use of energy resources to create jobs. A distinct society needs such measures. Quebec needs them. Canada, across the border from a society that is ten times as big as this country, needs such measures.
The free trade agreement with the United States relinquishes the power to use such measures, both at the federal and provincial level. Why become a distinct society under the terms of Meech Lake, without the tools to do the job?
I understand why the big corporations in the private sector support this agreement, especially the multinationals which rely on large imports from the United States. Any pressure to lower salaries and social benefits is very much to their advantage. Newspapers controlled by big corporations share this attitude. However, I fail to understand why Quebec's two major political parties have sided with the corporations against the interests of the vast majority of Quebecers. They must have overlooked those parts of the agreement that relinquish political power to the U.S. market.
I accuse this Government of abandoning all principles of honesty and fair play as far as this agreement is concerned. I accuse this Government of proceeding without a mandate from Canadian voters. I accuse the Conservative Government of relinquishing the political powers of the provinces and the federal Government to the economic forces of the U.S. market. On behalf of my Party I demand that an election be held as soon as possible.

We want an election. If ever there was a Government without a mandate, this is it. It has broken promises and attacked social programs. It has failed to achieve tax reform or bring in adequate child care programs. It has an appalling record on patronage and friends in high places. It has refused to plug the loopholes in election law and to bring in real controls in conflict of interest. Its trade deal has sold out Canada in our distinctive culture, our social programs, our natural resources and in the possibilities for industrial strategies, job creation and regional equalization.
May 16, 1988

For all of these reasons, I call on the House to condemn the Government and I call on the Government to go to the people of Canada by calling an election now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a great deal of what the Hon. Member said today is not exactly accurate. I will cover that later in my remarks.
All that the NDP and Liberals do is to knock the trade deal. Neither have come up with a policy-the Hon. Member from Montreal, a former Minister, holds a document. Have you read that?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
It certainly does not make any sense to us. It does not meet the realities of what is going on in the world today.
How does the NDP propose to handle the protectionist mood in the United States today? How does it plan to handle the various good Canadian industries that are under attack by special interest groups in the United States? How does the NDP propose to handle these problems in Canada?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not think giving up our political sovereignty and caving in time after time is a very good way to handle the problem. We heard constantly before this trade deal was signed that it would save us from the countervail powers of the United States. We were told it would be a trade deal to cut off the protectionist pressures in the United States. It did not achieve that.
We have seen the Government cave in time after time, with film distribution as the latest example of a government without the courage to pursue Canadian interests.
The Government has no mandate to act this way. Before the election it was against any kind of bilateral trade deal. It said clearly that it would not pursue that kind of option because Canada would be smashed. It used the elephant and the flea analogy. The Government's mandate was to oppose the trade deal. It does not have a mandate at all to pursue a trade deal.
What would we do positively? We have spoken frequently about what we would do. We issued a report stressing other objectives-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Like nationalization.
Supply

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Our report outlines possibilities for development of municipal infrastructure for local job creation, mechanisms to deal with irritants on a particular case basis. It is not a question of a bilateral deal that includes everything and in which we give up the power to act in the future. We would deal with matters on an industry by industry basis. We believe that is the safest way to proceed and also defend Canadian interests. It is a way to make sure that regional interests are not lost in the deal.
The Conservative Government has simply caved in in the hope that the friendship between the President and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will save us from U.S. protectionism. It has not saved us from any protectionist measure by the U.S. in the past and it will not in the future.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I understand the NDP policy on trade is to help municipalities with job creation. That is what the Hon. Member answered.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: One measure among many.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
The other measure she says is to handle them case by case as they attack our industries one by one. That is what she said.
That is what has been happening in the past and it has been costing industries in Canada millions and millions of dollars to defend those actions. The NDP policy is to perpetuate that. That is what the Hon. Member just told the House. I cannot believe it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: You are just going to cave in.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
The NDP are back in the 1960s. They do not want to change. They wear blinders so that they will not see what is happening around them. They want to look straight ahead rather than see what is happening. They are a bunch of standard bred horses with blinders. I might add that they are not breaking any track records with their attitude.
The NDP has no policy. We know what it opposes but we certainly do not know what it proposes.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member talks about being against change. What is most profoundly offensive about this so-called trade deal is that it prevents change in the future. It takes away the flexibility of the federal Government, provincial Governments or territorial Governments to make decisions because the deal binds future Governments. It states that we cannot use the political process 10, 20, 50 or 100 years from now when conditions may be different and a different strategy may be needed. We will not be able to use a different strategy because the decision has been made.
For example, there has not been nearly enough discussion on the section dealing with monopolies. There has been a cover-up on the part of the Government because it does not want Canadians to know what it has given away.

May 16, 1988
Supply
The section on monopolies provides for a dispute settlement by a panel on which we do not control the membership. We would be a minority on that panel.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Wait a minute.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Horsefeathers.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: We have two Canadians, two Americans and a fifth person chosen by them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Chosen by whom?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Chosen by two Canadians and two Americans.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Where does the panelist come from?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: We have no idea.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: It could be the Chairman of GATT.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
We have no idea who the fifth person would be. We know further that the panel reports to a trade disputes commission, the Canada-U.S. Trade Commission. We do not know how many members would be on this commission in terms of people, but there are two parties to it. It could be the two trade ministers. Their decisions would be made on the basis of so-called consensus. How can there be a consensus with just two bodies, one of which is 10 times more powerful than the other? What kind of recourse do we have when that body says: "Do it our way or else?" We are trapped in that decision. We cannot develop another strategy because we are bound to it.
It is not like the system in Europe which has a Parliament with permanent institutions involving a variety of countries that give their power to a whole.
We are giving our power to a neighbour 10 times larger and 10 times more powerful than us. We will not be able to stand up to their demands.
Therefore, the Government is closing off options for the future and taking away decisions that should be made in this Parliament and the legislatures of the provinces and the territories, decisions that should be made by local councils, Indian bands, all of these citizens who have minds and hearts, and care about Canada. It is giving away that power to panels and a commission that we do not control either now or in the future.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Member knows that I have much respect for her. However, I say with great respect that what she has said this morning represents, if anything, the line of Bob White and the Canadian Auto Workers. I suggest to her that it is anathema to the outer eight provinces in Canada and those who work in the forestry and mining industries in British Columbia.
Let me confine the argument to her own Province of Ontario. Does she realize that if the trade agreement is not
ratified, the Auto Pact can be cancelled on one year's notice? Does she realize that the trade agreement would enshrine the Auto Pact so that if it is cancelled, everything would be cancelled? In that sense, it provides protection for the 100,000 or more people who work in the automobile industry in Ontario.
Does she realize that we have had free trade in the auto industry since 1968, other than for a few months in the early 1980s when Chrysler was in trouble? Fortunately, Ontario has been the great beneficiary of that free trade.
Is Mr. White not saying that what has worked so well in Ontario with respect to the auto industry is something that must not happen in other parts of Canada?
Will she deal with the argument relating to the Auto Pact?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Auto Pact can be cancelled, as the whole trade deal can be cancelled, according to the terms. It is not free trade in the automobile sector. It is managed trade with the possibility of the reintroduction of tariffs if investment is not made according to what is specified. It is very, very different. Here we are going to be wide open to investment going both ways. We lose the protections. We lose the penalties in this trade deal that we previously had in the Auto Pact.
The Auto Pact was not supposed to be on the bargaining table. We ought to have more Auto Pacts. That is the kind of thing we should be pursuing on an industry by industry basis so that other parts of the country can profit from it.
The Hon. Member refers to British Columbia and Alberta. All the provinces lose political sovereignty. All the provinces lose the power to make decisions about natural resources. Natural resources are supposed to be a provincial responsibility, according to our Constitution. By having a continental approach to resources, it is giving away the provincial jurisdiction over resources we have in our Constitution. That means that the federal Government is assuming that jurisdiction illegally, in my opinion, and handing it over to the Americans in a continental energy pact. That is flagrantly wrong.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
The time provided for questions and comments has now expired. Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace- Lachine East (Mr. Allmand).

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Madam Speaker, the Liberal Party fully supports this motion before the House today because it restates the position the Liberal Party has taken with respect to this bad trade deal ever since it was revealed to the public last year. We have said over and over again that this trade deal between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the President of the United States threatens our present social programs, our medicare,
May 16, 1988

health care, family allowances and old age pensions and limits our ability to bring in new social programs such as day care, and so on.
We also say that this bad trade deal threatens other social programs and programs related to social life in Canada such as marketing boards, affirmative action programs, environmental programs, and in a moment I will spell out exactly how that will happen. Even this morning, in answer to questions from the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, our Leader, the Right Hon. John Turner, made it very clear again, that is our position, and that is why we will support this motion today.
Before I get into the substance of the matter, I want to respond immediately to the question put by the Hon. Member from Brampton to our colleague in the New Democratic Party. He asked: "What is your alternative if you do not do it our way?" Well, the Liberal Party has published an alternative and I stated it in an ad lib way when he was posing his question to the Hon. Member, to which he replied: "Well, it is not worth anything". First he says we do not have an alternative, and when I point out very clearly that we do, he then dismisses it. Of course, he will dismiss it because it completely disagrees with his approach on these matters.
What is our alternative? It is to pursue trade barriers through the multilateral process and through the sector process. I want to point out that it has worked in the past. We cannot understand why the Conservative Government would change that pattern, that approach, and in doing so give up vital elements of our sovereignty and independence.
Let us look at the record. Since the end of the Second World War, mostly under Liberal Governments, we have been able to reduce tariffs between Canada and the United States to the point where approximately 80 per cent of all goods and services now move between the United States and Canada without tariffs. That was done through the Kennedy Round, through the Uruguay Round, through the Tokyo Round. It was done through multilateral bargaining to the point where 80 per cent of our goods and services now move between these two countries without tariffs. In addition, when we started this process back in the 1940s and 1950s, the average tariffs between Canada and the United States were about 29 per cent. They have been reduced to about 7 per cent only on the 20 per cent remaining goods and services. That is a pretty successful record in lowering tariff barriers.
The major outstanding barrier that remains between Canada and the United States is not the tariff barrier. It is important but it was going down anyway. The remaining outstanding barrier is countervail. This deal between the Prime Minister and the President does nothing about countervail. It is the most harassing barrier against Canadian business and traders, and this agreement does not do one thing about it. When the Conservative Government started out, that was its goal, to get some sort of agreement that would reduce the applicability of countervail by the Government of the United
Supply
States against our Canadian business and traders. That was not done.
When Members opposite ask for our alternatives, I find it quite amusing. I like to put these quotes on the record as often as I can. During the Conservative leadership campaign in 1983, what did leading Conservatives say about a possible free trade deal with the United States? In 1983, before the election of 1984, the Prime Minister said: "Canadians rejected free trade with the United States in 1911. They would do so again in 1983. Canada must increase its share of total world trade which has dropped by 33 per cent in the past two decades". The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said: "Bilateral free trade with the United States is simplistic and naive. It would only serve to further diminish our ability to compete internationally". What a flip-flop. That is what was said in 1983, and in 1985 they are saying exactly the opposite.
The former Minister of State, the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), said about a potential free trade agreement with the United States: "It is silly. Canada must improve relations in trade with the United States, of course, but our natural destiny is to become a global leader, not America's weak sister". Is that not a great statement? No wonder he left the Cabinet. I suppose he was feeling uneasy about some of these things and thought he would take the honourable way out.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in 1983, at the very same leadership convention, which was manoeuvred by the Prime Minister to get rid of Mr. Clark, said the following: "Unrestrained free trade with the United States raises the possibility that thousands of jobs could be lost in such critical industries as textiles, furniture and footwear". This is what the leading members of the Conservative Cabinet said in 1983 about a so-called free trade agreement with the United States. That was one year before the election of 1984, and in the 1984 election campaign they did not give us one hint they would pursue this kind of agreement which threatens our social, environmental, affirmative action policies, and so on.
What did happen? Our Prime Minister, at the first opportunity, went down to Washington and did an Irish jig with the President of the United States and they patted each other on the back and drank champagne. The Prime Minister jumped right into the President's pocket and there he was ready to accept anything the President proposed to him. We ended up negotiating the free trade deal which will sell out our sovereignty and independence unless we defeat it.
This so-called free trade agreement, and I call it "so-called" because it is not really a classical free trade agreement, not only limits our ability to decide on new social programs in the future but threatens our present social programs. How does it do it? It does it in two ways.

May 16, 1988
Supply
[DOT] (U50)
First, it does it directly since it forbids, in many ways, subsidized programs. The Americans like to have what is called a level playing field. That means that all businesses must compete without any subsidy and under the same rules no matter whether they are big, small, new or old, and regardless of what their hold is on the market-place. With that sort of clause in the free trade agreement our regional development policies are threatened. Our marketing boards are threatened, as are our environmental programs. They all involve subsidies to small businesses, to start up businesses and so on. That in turn affects our social policy, particularly in the slow-growth areas of Canada such as Atlantic Canada, the North, some of the prairie provinces, and northern Quebec. That is how the deal directly threatens social programs and the levels of social welfare in Canada.
However, it also attacks them indirectly, and in this regard I mentioned some of the programs. I mentioned our health programs, our minimum wage, our unemployment insurance program, our old age pensions, and others. It attacks them indirectly because there will be very strong pressure to harmonize our Canadian programs with American programs.
How will that happen? Let us look at some of the testimony that was given to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade by certain big businesses. I am referring particularly to McCain's. My hon. colleague behind me is from New Brunswick. He knows what McCain's said about the deal. I also refer to the President of Quaker Oats.
These people have said the following. At the present time in Canada they buy their raw food materials for food products which are processed from marketing boards. They have said that they do not oppose marketing boards in general. They feel that they are good for farmers since they give them a steady and fair income over the years. However, they said, if this deal is brought in and they as food processors have to compete with American companies that do not have to buy their raw food products from marketing boards and they can sell to Canada without tariffs, then they will be at an unfair advantage. They said: "We are against marketing boards in that particular environment. You will have to get rid of the marketing boards so that we can buy our raw food products on the free market, or we will move to the United States where we will have access to the Canadian market since there will be no tariffs or barriers".
What this agreement has done is to have put some of our food processors into a position in which they say: "Either get rid of marketing boards or we go to the United States". That is what it has done. At the present time they are not facing that dilemma. We are suggesting to the Government that it should not have put these companies in front of that dilemma.
The same is true about many other programs since Canadian companies that have their plants and head offices here in Canada will have to compete on this so-called level playing
field with American companies that have lower social programs in the United States, lower minimum wages to pay, and lower unemployment insurance. Yet our Canadian companies that have to pay the taxes to support these social programs, which we believe are important, will say at one point: "Because we are in Canada, we are paying taxes to our provincial and federal Governments to support important social programs. We have always paid those taxes and we have not objected to them. But now, because we have to compete with American companies that are not paying taxes to support medicare and a reasonable unemployment insurance system, those companies are coming into Canada and underselling us". These Canadian companies will say to the Government: "Either you reduce these programs so we can compete, or we will go to the United States".
The pressure will arise. I might say that that sort of pressure arose when we were discussing the Bill on pharmaceutical drugs during the last year. People in Montreal were saying: "Either you support the Government's Bill to weaken support for reasonable drug prices or we are going to do our research and development in the United States or some other country". They were trying to put that pressure on us even then. But of course the Government had made this deal with the United States. It pushed through its Bill despite the objections on this side of the House. We have now seen drug prices go up in Canada for ordinary Canadians. Already they are paying the price for the Government's policy on free trade.
I have already mentioned with respect to jobs-I forget how much time I have left, Madam Speaker. I could spend the whole day attacking this agreement.
With respect to jobs-

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: In Montreal, in the pharmaceutical industry.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
I have dealt with that. The Government has already raised the price of pharmaceuticals through its Bill. We will be watching to see how much research and development and new employment there will be in Canada as a result of it. We have not seen it yet, but we will be watching very closely. With respect to that Bill, we had a formula as a result of a commission that would have solved the problem without selling out to the United States. So there was another way of doing that without pursuing the same means that the Government put before us.
This trade deal with the United States is a means of entrenching a Conservative agenda for a long period of time. That is the hidden side of it. What this agreement will do is more or less to entrench us into a free market system with a Conservative agenda, an agenda against reasonable social programs, minimum wages, unemployment insurance and affirmative action programs. Once we get into this deal with the United States it will be hard to change. The sort of society which prevails in the United States will be imported into
May 16, 1988

Canada through this deal. For the Government to suggest otherwise is complete nonsense.
When a country of 25 million people, Canada, is up against a country of 250 million people, the United States, one does not need much intelligence to conclude who will win. It certainly would be nice if the Americans would harmonize to our medicare programs, to our hospitalization programs, to our unemployment insurance system and so on, but they will not. The pressure on Canadian companies will be to do it the same way as they do it in the United States so that we can compete.
Very often the Government likes to compare the Canada-U.S. trade deal with the European Common Market. It says: "Look, free trade works in Europe, therefore, this is a great deal. It is similar, it will work here. The Canada-U.S. trade deal is not at all the same as the Common Market. First, the European Common Market involves a large number of countries. Several of them are larger countries, such as Britain, Germany, France and Italy. There are some smaller countries, such as the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Denmark, and others. They all have their own languages and their own cultures. There is not the opportunity for any one of those countries to overwhelm the other. The Germans will not overwhelm the French, and the French will not overwhelm the English. They balance each other off so that one side will not predominate.
Unfortunately, in this particular deal we have a country of 25 million people, Canada, in which two-thirds of the people speak English. We are already bombarded by American magazines, television, films and so on. We are side by side with a country of 250 million people who speak the same language as two-thirds of our own people. The threats that are present in this one-on-one deal are not present in the European Common Market. One cannot compare the Common Market to this particular deal. Nor can it be compared to the Auto Pact. The Auto Pact is not a free trade deal. It is a managed trade deal. It obliges the United States to invest in Canada. It obliges the United States to maintain so many jobs in Canada. It is a managed trade deal. It does not allow the United States to do whatever it wants with respect to these matters.
With respect to jobs, we have all sorts of estimates. I suppose that jobs are the ultimate social policy. One's policy on employment is one's ultimate social policy because the first goal is to have people working in good, solid jobs. There are safety nets in case they are not working, for example, if a worker is ill, handicapped or thrown out of work.
There have been so many statements with respect to jobs. One day the former Minister of Employment said that 300,000 jobs would be lost. The next day he retracted on that and was contradicted by the Minister of Finance. There have been all sorts of estimates. Some were that we would lose jobs, and some were that we would gain them. The most recent one, about a month ago, in a report of the Economic Council stated that over a 10-year period we would have a net gain of over
Supply
200,000 jobs. That is an average of 20,000 to 25,000 jobs per year in all of Canada. That is what was said we would gain.
The report pointed out-and a great many people did not look into the fine print of that report-that 188,000 jobs would be lost. Most of those jobs are in industry. Most of the jobs that would be gained are in the service sector. We all know that, for the most part, in industry the jobs are high paying, full time, unionized, with benefits, pensions, and so on. The jobs that will replace them under this deal will be nonunionized, minimum wage, part-time, and involve contracting out. That is the American way; lay off full-time workers and contract out to a small company that can avoid the minimum standards of national programs. They will hire the same people to do the job whether it is maintenance or repairs, and it will be done at the minimum wage, whereas before it was done for a reasonable wage where a man could support his family. That is what will happen as a result of this deal. There will be good industrial jobs lost to service type jobs in this wild melee with the United States over trade and markets.
Despite this adjustment that will have to take place between industrial type jobs and service type jobs, it is interesting to note that the Government has not provided for any special retraining or adjustment programs. Two committees of the House, in unanimous reports, recommended special adjustment programs. That means that the Conservative Members on those committees agreed with those reports, because they have the majority.
In the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration there are five Conservatives, one Liberal, and one New Democrat. Together, the seven of us issued a report stating that there must be special adjustment programs in order that the person who has been kicked out of an industrial job and has to go into a service type job will have some type of retraining.
What did the Government say when we asked for those special adjustment and training programs? It stated that the present programs are good enough. People all over the country are saying that they are not good enough. Last week the community colleges in Toronto said that the Canadian job strategy was not adequate. They stated that they could not train people to fill the jobs in Toronto at the present time where there is a very good economy. They said that they cannot even get the people trained to do those jobs.
The reason that the Canadian job strategy is not doing the work that it should do is that the Government has cut training programs by 32 per cent since 1984. In 1984 those programs received $2.2 billion, and now they are down to $1.6 billion. That is the type of programming that will be used to adjust workers who are thrown out of good jobs when the free trade agreement goes into effect. No, Madam Speaker.
I wish to reiterate that we support this resolution. The trade deal threatens our social programs. It threatens our job

May 16, 1988

policies. It threatens our cultural programs. This agreement is not only about trade, and it is not only an economic agreement. This is a deal with very serious social and political implications. The real question in this debate, not only here today but throughout the months to come, is what type of country do we want. What type of place do we want Canada to be? What is our vision and dream for Canada? Is it a Canada that is a semi-sovereign appendage of the United States, harmonized to United States standards, harmonized to United States social programs and culture? Is it submitting to the doctrine of manifest destiny which was enunciated in the United States over 100 years ago? Or is our vision of Canada of a free, independent Canada, friendly with the United States and other countries but developing its own policies, pursuing its own goals, maintaining its own identity and sovereignty? That is what this debate is about. My choice is with the latter option, and we will completely oppose this agreement to the bitter end.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
I agree with a great deal of what the Hon. Member had said about condemning the Government on this trade deal. I particularly agree with the Hon. Member on his interpretation of the trade deal as bringing in the Conservative agenda, that the Government would not have the nerve to attack our social programs and our cultural institutions in a direct manner. Therefore, in this indirect manner it is able to pursue the neo-Conservative agenda along with Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher. I heartily agree with all of that.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member why, given the concerns that he has raised in his speech, Quebec Liberals are not opposing the trade deal? It seems that because of the loss of sovereignty, the loss of power to make decisions, to pursue the distinct society, to use performance requirements, to have a provincial energy policy as opposed to a continental energy strategy, to use the energy sector for job creation, to have a differential pricing policy, and all of those things that Quebec has used effectively in the past, under the trade deal Quebec will lose the opportunity to make those types of decisions. I wonder why Quebec Liberals are not fighting with the Hon. Member against the trade deal.
My final question is the following. With the increasingly hypothetical possibility of the Liberals forming a federal Government in the near future, how can we be sure that they would tear up the trade deal? Some days they say that they would tear it up, and on other days they are not so sure that they would. What type of day would it have to be for the Liberals to decide one way or the other on this absolutely crucial question for the future survival of Canada?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
I wish to make it clear that it is the Quebec Government, a government of the Quebec Liberal Party, which has taken that position. There are many Liberals in Quebec who take the same position as the federal Liberal Party which means that they oppose the deal. The Government of Robert Bourassa supports the deal. If the Hon. Member is asking me to explain why they are supporting the deal, I am
afraid that I cannot explain why Mr. Bourassa is supporting the deal, because I do not agree with him. Unfortunately, I take issue with Mr. Bourassa on this. By the way, the Liberal Party, different from the New Democratic Party, has two separate Parties in Quebec. There is the Quebec Liberal Party and the federal Liberal Party in Quebec. A large number of people belong to both Parties. The reason they split years ago was that things are often seen from a federal perspective or a provincial perspective.
Having said that, I guess one would have to elicit the reason for the Quebec Government supporting the deal. I feel that the deal is contrary to the interests of Quebec; Quebec farmers are opposing the deal, Quebec workers are opposing the deal. If energy is the principal reason why Mr. Bourassa is supporting the deal, I do not see that as a legitimate reason. Mr. Bourassa is already selling a good deal of Quebec energy to the United States. It is true that he has to respect the mechanisms of the Energy Board, as long as it stays in place., The fact of the matter is that I do not know how this would help Quebec in promoting its energy business.
On the other hand, I think it would hurt Quebec citizens since they may not be able to have a lower price for their own energy as they have had for years. It has always been a natural thing to do that if there is a lot of electricity, oil or gas, the citizens of that province receive a lower price. We have been benefiting in Quebec from low hydro prices for many years. If I understand the deal correctly, and many experts have told me that this is the case, we will not be able to charge one price to Quebecers for energy and another price to Americans. The same price will have to be charged. Therefore, if a market in the United States dictates a higher price, then that is what we will have to pay in Quebec. I am not an apologist for the Quebec Government of Robert Bourassa, and I cannot tell the Hon. Member what his arguments are. In any case, I do not support those arguments.
The other point raised by the Hon. Member was that on one day we say that we will tear up the agreement, and on another day we say we will not. I would like the Hon. Member to cite the days when our Leader has stated that he would not. He states that, if elected to office, as the Leader of the Party and as the Prime Minister of the day, he would tell the United States that this deal is not acceptable to us and we want out. He has stated that over and over again. I do not know what the Hon. Member is talking about when she says on some days he states that he would tear up the agreement and on other days he states the opposite.
I challenge her and anybody else in this House or elsewhere to show me one quote from the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner) where he would agree to this trade deal. He said over and over again that he will not agree to this trade deal, that he prefers the alternatives set out in our Liberal Party booklet called "Reaching Out. A Liberal alternative to the Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement", which is to pursue lower
May 16, 1988

tariffs and lower trade barriers internationally through the multilateral process and through sector agreements as we have done for years and years with great success.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me comment on my hon. friend's discussion. I think everybody in this House wants a free and independent Canada. We want a free and prosperous Canada, but we also want a Canada able to afford its social programs, own cultural programs and its own sovereignty. The choice is not between the status quo, as many would have you believe, Madam Speaker, and free trade with the United States; the choice is really between a competitive, vigorous Canada and a Canada which will sink into an abyss of protectionism and government intervention to make us uncompetitive in the whole world. That is what this is all about.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Member to give me the article number.
Second, could he give me the article number where it says that we cannot protect our cultural industries and cannot continue to promote the CBC, where we cannot subsidize all the things we have been subsidizing now, and where the United States cannot take reciprocal action. Canada has developed one of the best social networks in the world without a free trade agreement with the United States.

In this country we have developed excellent social programs without a free trade deal with the United States and over the years Canadians have ensured good jobs and prosperity. As a matter of fact, in the last year for which we have trade figures Canada had a $200 billion trade surplus with the United States. Yet the Government was begging for this free trade agreement with the United States which gives up our sovereignty and threatens our social programs.
The Hon. Member asked me where in the agreement it says that certain social programs are threatened or our ability to bring in new programs is limited.

speechtext: What about electricity?

I will deal with electricity. Of course it does not say that explicitly, but I refer to the the testimony of the people from Quaker Oats, the people from McCains and others who have said that if they are to compete with American companies in Canada they will not be able to afford the taxes and special payments which they make for these social programs if they compete with these companies which do not have that same infrastructure.
With respect to energy, what the agreement does say-I have the elements of the agreement here and I will have somebody here this afternoon with the final agreement-is that there is broad agreement to ensure the freest possible bilateral trade in energy, including non-discriminatory access for the United States to Canadian energy supplies and secure market access for Canadian energy exports to the United States.
One has to ask, and many experts have, what does nondiscriminatory access by the United States to Canadian energy supplies mean? It means that you cannot charge a higher price to Americans than to Canadians. I will go on with the elements of agreement at page 17. It states that both sides have agreed to prohibit restrictions on imports or exports including quantitative restrictions, taxes, minimum import or export price requirements or any other equivalent measure subject to very limited exceptions. It goes on. If the Americans are to have non-discriminatory access to our energy supplies, then it means we cannot charge them a higher price than we charge Canadians.
By the way, Peter Lougheed, former Premier of Alberta, was asked that question when he came to the committee chaired by the Hon. Member. He said, "Despite the fact that we will not be able to give Albertans a lower price for oil and gas because of this deal, I still support it because, on the balance", according to him, "it was a good deal". He supported it despite the fact that he would not be able to give a lower price to Albertans for oil and gas and other energy supplies in that province. That is what Lougheed said to the committee. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has been a very interesting morning so far as we have listened to the spokespersons for the New Democratic and the Liberal Parties trying to outdo one another in undermining Canada's position as a trading nation. Obviously they are completely, introverted in their outlook. It does not say anything much for the future of the country when we get such a narrow introverted policy being espoused by members of the opposition Parties.
Within a few days now the House of Commons will debate in earnest the free trade agreement which was negotiated between Canada and the United States. If what I have heard so far from Hon. Members opposite is any indication of that debate, then I think it will have less to do with the future of Canada and more with the election hopes of the New Democratic and Liberal Parties.
In fact, as I read this motion and as I listen to the arguments put forward so far I really do not have any sense that Members in the Opposition really believe what it is they are saying simply because they know just how ludicrous their claims are. But I very much have a sense that they want the people of Canada to believe what they are saying. They want Canadians to believe that the Government would abandon its social or its cultural policies despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary that has been shown time and time again. But one thing stands in the way, the truth. Not a version of the truth, not a perception of the truth but the truth, plain and simple. That is really what the people of Canada are seeing. The truth proves indisputably, clearly, that Canada's sovereignty, Canada's right to establish and expand our social policies and cultural policies is as strong today six months after the agreement was signed as it ever has been.
Of course, the New Democratic Party is not about to let a little thing like the truth stand in the way. New Democrats want people to be frightened. That is the aim. They want people to doubt the future of this country, especially those in our society who are the most vulnerable, our older Canadians on fixed incomes, single parent mothers and children, Canadians on disability pensions and veterans' pensions, and Canadians in job retraining programs who rely on child care allowances in order to learn new skills. These are the people to whom their remarks are directed in the hope that they will create fear and concern among them. However, the truth sets out quite clearly what has been the trend in Canada over the last 50 years.
For the last 50 years, Canada and the United States have been progressively liberalizing trade between our two countries. Today, just 15 per cent of our trade carries any sort of tariff or any sort of restriction. The other 85 per cent is
already free, and one must ask oneself what exactly is the result of these 50 years during which we have been reducing trade barriers to arrive at 85 per cent of our trade free. What exactly has happened? Have we seen our social programs diminished? Have we seen our powers limited in any way? Of course not. The exact opposite to that has occurred.
This half century has been marked by the greatest progression forward of social and cultural policies in our history. Programs such as medicare which is available to every Canadian, the Canada Pension Plan with disability allowances and survivors' benefits, the spouse's allowance, the child tax credit and many, many others. These have all been implemented during the time when our trade with the United States has been progressively liberalized.
What holds true for Canada's social programs also holds true for our cultural programs. Obviously, we have been introducing programs in both fields over this period of time when our trade has been liberalized to the point where only 15 per cent remain with any kind of barriers, tariffs or restrictions.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Through the multilateral process.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Through bilateral and multilateral processes.
The fact is, and the record will prove, that the free trade agreement with the United States guarantees and strengthens the bonds of Canadian culture and identity by writing into the agreement a special exemption for culture. As with social programs, it is precisely the last 50 years, in which we have seen trade barriers and tariffs being reduced between the two countries, that we have seen as well an establishment and growth of independent and viable cultural industries and institutions in Canada. Because they are independent and because they are here, we insisted on having exemptions in the field of culture. We do have an independent culture, a culture that we can be proud of, one that we want to see grow, because it is so very special to each and every one of us.
This, of course, brings me back to this petty-minded motion that is before us today. Those who support this motion show that they have not understood the first principles, not only of the exemptions but of our Canadian culture itself. What do the cultural exemptions which Canada insisted upon in the free trade agreement mean? The exemptions mean that Canada will use support and policy measures to promote the financial viability of Canada's cultural industries, whether they involve individual artists or large organizations. Our purpose is to promote the ability of Canada's creators to reach the Canadian audience.
Opposition Members are so tied up with relying on what Americans have to say that they forget the purpose of our cultural policies. Cultural industries are exempted because the arbitration of continental market forces alone, with economics of scale determining success, should not govern whether an adequate Canadian choice is available in our lives.
May 16, 1988

The exemptions mean that Canadian content rules will continue to apply in broadcasting policy. They mean that simultaneous substitution and Bill C-58 as it applies to advertising will remain cornerstones of the Canadian broadcasting system. Why is this? It is because we insisted that those exemptions should be there.
The exemptions mean that the CBC will remain a central figure in the way our cultural growth and development take place, as with the Canada Council and our other cultural institutions. Every one of them is free to develop as they and the Government of the day see fit. Why is this? Again, because we were determined to see that all of these industries and agencies were exempted from the free trade agreement.
The exemptions mean that our publishing industry will continue to grow and prosper under majority ownership, because the Baie Comeau policy is preserved intact. In fact, if anything, free trade strengthens the policy by insisting that when there is no other Canadian purchaser available, the Canadian Government itself will pay fair market price for a foreign-owned publishing concern that is required to be sold under the divestiture terms of the policy. That is a new and even better guarantee for our publishing industry, and we have done that in the case of Ginn and Company.
I might also observe that the Baie Comeau policy has now been applied on four different occasions, directly or indirectly. It has been applied on Doubleday, Holt, Rinehart & Winston, Ginn and GLC. However, I might say that we are not in the business of protecting warehouses, whether American or British, as in the case of the Penguin takeover of NAL. Instead, we have directed our attention to the retention of postal subsidies and to the retention of Bill C-58 as it applies to advertising because these too are part of our exemptions. That, of course, is what Hon. Members opposite seem to forget.
These exemptions strengthen and secure the roots of a thriving Canadian culture, no matter what opponents may claim to the contrary. It is thriving, because for the last three and a half years, this Government has made an unprecedented commitment to an independent and secure cultural future for Canada, equal to and, in the opinion of many, surpassing anything that has been done before. Opposition MPs, of course, pull no punches when telling the people of Canada what the Government has failed to do in this area, or what they think it has failed to do.
Just let me give Hon. Members a brief sampler of the things that have been done. If Hon. Members object to these, I would like to see them rise and say so. It is this Government which set up the Canadian sound recording development program, a program to give Canadians an opportunity to hear their own singers, their own songwriters, their own composers and their own musicians. For the next five years, $25 million has been put into this program, and it is having tremendous benefits.
It is this Government which created the Public Lending Right Program, something for which writers had argued for 40
Supply
years. This Government brought in a program that has given long overdue recognition and compensation to Canada's writers for the public use of their works.
It is this Government which established the Baie Comeau publishing policy to ensure Canadian control of this vital industry. It is this Government which created the book publishing industry development fund. We have moved to strengthen Canada's national museums and their contributions to cultural activity all across Canada.
It is this Government which achieved what no other Government in over 60 years has achieved, that is, to begin revision of the Copyright Act which is so absolutely vital to our creators. If Liberal Members opposite would just convince their colleagues in the Senate to pass the copyright Bill we will provide a greater guarantee for creators than we have seen in this country heretofore.
It is also this Government which made the broadcast program production fund an ongoing program involving $60 million every year. It has made Telefilm Canada a major producer of quality Canadian programming. We have also created a separate five-year $165 million fund for feature films. It is this Government which accomplished what other Governments only talked about, an independent film distribution system. This is not a record of abandonment or limitation. It is not a record of faint measures. I might add for the benefit of Hon. Members opposite that much of this was achieved in the past two years precisely while negotiations for a free trade agreement were going on.
There are others who say what I have just said as well. It is not just I. In an editorial last autumn the Winnipeg Free Press said that "Canadian authors have enjoyed national and international success. More Canadian plays have been appearing in Canadian regional theatres. A host of Canadian ballet companies have sprung up. Canadian films have begun to make their way on to Canadian and foreign scenes. Canadian television programs are finding larger Canadian audiences. Certainly if culture expression is any measure, the Canadian identity has never been stronger". Never stronger, Madam Speaker, directly because of the contributions and initiatives of this Government.
Let us look at what has happened since the signing of the free trade agreement and its tabling in the House. Just look at that period of time alone. If the agreement signals, as Hon. Members opposite would say, the "voluntary relinquishing" of Canadian sovereignty to decide upon newer expanded cultural programs, then surely we would see some indication of this. Yet what do we see instead? Just take a look at the last six months in the Department of Communications alone. We have increased the public lending rights to authors by some $800,000. We have increased grants paid out through the Canada Council by $8 million. We have announced the go-ahead on the CBC's new broadcast centre in Toronto. CBC

May 16, 1988
Supply
resources have increased this year by $53 million. In fact, total program spending in this portfolio will increase by $115 million this fiscal year alone.
The new Canadian film distribution program, as I have already said, has accomplished what no Government before ever attempted. That is, we have created a separate national film distribution market by governing the importation of foreign films. That is something which has been requested for years. The Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) may not want that measure in Canada, but those of us who believe in the future of Canadian culture and films certainly do.
That policy, of course, does even more than establish rules giving access by Canadian distributors to independently produced films. It also creates a $85 million film distribution fund to help Canadian distributors achieve this objective and invest in and market Canadian-produced films. The program also gives another $115 million to Telefilm Canada and the National Film Board to make culturally significant Canadian films over the next five years. Again, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood may not want to see that come into effect, but those in the Canadian film industry do. As Peter Simpson, President of Norstar Distributors said, it is a terrific piece of legislation. The people in the industry know.
Then there is another program, that of postal subsidies. Canada's publishing industry sees this Government's billion dollar plus commitment to continue postal subsidies as yet one more affirmation, one more proof, that this Government has lived up to its word on culture and free trade. It is building for the future. Governments have traditionally renewed postal subsidies one year at a time. We have moved to give the publishing industry long-term security and stability by announcing that this program will continue in effect for the next five years so they are able to plan adequately.
What we have done in film programs we have done in the field of sound recording and so many other fields. Only Members opposite cannot see what we have accomplished and what the industry recognizes as the contribution made to them. The reason they cannot see that is that they do not have either the foresight or hindsight, they only have the short-sightedness to look at themselves, what it is they want to carp about at any particular time, with no policies whatsoever in this field.
In closing, I want to say that the evidence that we have respected and lived up to in the free trade agreement with regard to culture is all around us. We see it reflected in the industries as they grow and develop and become stronger. Others during this day will speak to some of the issues raised this morning. I close merely by saying that fear and the creation of fear will get Hon. Members opposite nowhere because Canadians understand the game they are playing. Canadians understand what it is they are trying to do and they simply will not buy it.

Madam Speaker, at the beginning of her remarks the Minister acknowledged that over the last 40 years there has been a considerable decrease in tariffs between Canada and the U.S. My figures show that at the present time about 80 per cent of goods and services are without tariff. She said, about 85 per cent. She also acknowledged that during that period of time there was a great increase in social and cultural programs. What she did not say was that all that was done without a special comprehensive trade agreement with the U.S.
If we were able to bring down tariffs to the extent that she acknowledges without a special bilateral comprehensive trade agreement with the U.S., why is it necessary to enter into such an agreement in order to get these decreases in tariffs?
In order to get further decreases in tariffs we have to give them, one, non-discriminatory access to our energy supplies. We have to treat all American companies as nationals. We have had to abolish our capacity to screen foreign investment to control U.S. investment in Canada. In order to get further tariff reductions we had to throw our agricultural industry into the same market-place as the Americans, even though we have long and harsh winters with all the costs associated with them. We had to weaken the Auto Pact.
Why was it necessary to enter into such an agreement when we were getting lower tariffs over the last 40 years without such a comprehensive agreement, without selling out our energy, our ability to screen foreign investment, our agriculture, and the Auto Pact? Why was it necessary to enter into such an agreement when we were getting these things through another process which was effective?

speakerposition: Minister of Communications

Madam Speaker, I know that the Hon. Member is a student of history and he may want to look back at the beginning of this arrangement whereby we have seen, over the past 50 odd years, the liberalization of trade between Canada and the United States.
It began in 1935 with the signing of the Most Favoured Nation Treaty between Canada and the United States. At that time that was the largest trading arrangement between any two countries in the history of the world. That Most Favoured Nation Treaty went on to become the forerunner of the GATT. After World War II that agreement between Canada and the United States became the prototype for the establishment of the GATT.
We have progressively followed that route bilaterally and multilaterally over the past 50 years. With the free trade agreement we now see the possibility for history to repeat itself, for the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States to become another model for the GATT with

May 16, 1988

regard to the liberalization of world trade which most countries desire. That is what the Uruguay Round is all about. In fact, we can help to move that process forward as we did in 1935 when we signed the Most Favoured Nation Treaty between our two great countries.

Madam Speaker, I remember when the Hon. Minister was an ardent nationalist and an activist within the Committee for an Independent Canada. I would have thought that she would be the Conservative who would lead the exodus from the Conservative Party over this trade deal. I thought that she would stand up for Canada and fight the deal instead of succumbing. She is today defending the indefensible, and I would like to ask her some very specific questions.
She talked about Bill C-58 but she did not talk about Article 2007, the print in Canada requirement which says that Canada shall repeal various sections of the Income Tax Act which define a Canadian issue of a newspaper or periodical for purposes of deduction of income tax expenses. This was the very controversial measure brought in to give a boost to magazine periodical publishing to encourage advertisers to advertise in Canadian publications.
Without this measure we probably would not have had the weekly Maclean's. Maclean's thinks it can do just fine without it in the future, but I do not think it could have got started without it. Certainly it only went weekly after we got that. Many magazines, which constitute a thriving industry in Canada now, depend on that. Would the Hon. Member comment about the pressure she has received from the smaller magazines especially which provide a very important cultural service for Canada and would want that?
She talks about the exemption for the cultural industries but it is a fairly limited list. Printing is not on the list. I wonder what Gutenberg would think about the suggestion that printing is not an artistic cultural activity. What about a province that wants to improve and develop book publishing within its own jurisdiction? What if it wants to see more Canadian publishing? We know it is important to get more textbook publishing done in Canada and some provinces, particularly Ontario, have had a printing policy. Would it be possible for a province to have a requirement that school textbooks be printed within the country, or would this be against the trade deal?
With regard to film distribution and ownership, the Minister has talked about her scheme, which is a very pale imitation even of the one about which she spoke a year ago. That, itself, was a far paler imitation of what had been recommended by the task force set up by her predecessor, that is, to have film distribution Canadian-owned.
My question on this is very specific. I cannot see the Liberals doing this because they have chickened out on this issue so often in the past, but if Party X gets into government and wants to bring in a film distribution ownership scheme,
