would that be against the trade deal? Would Canada be able to stand up on that issue.
What does it mean when the Government of the United States, in its summary of the free trade agreement, states very explicitly:
However, the U.S. retains the right to redress any adverse commercial effects of any future cultural measures enacted by Canada.
Would the Hon. Minister tell us what kind of future cultural measures the United States Government might have in mind? This is not fear-mongering. What are these future cultural measures that the United States would be able to stop as a result of this shameful trade deal?

The Member has asked about Section 2005. She cites this Section as being somehow sinister to Canada's cultural purposes and undermining the significance of the cultural exemption. Since she does not seem to be able to recognize this, I will explain to her that this is both a clarification and a protection. On the one hand, it makes clear that since cultural industries are exempt under the agreement the dispute settlement mechanism specified in the agreement generally does not apply. For actions taken by one side or another in the area of cultural industries the existing trade remedy laws continue to apply, as they have in the past.
The difference is that while in the past the U.S. could take counter measures of any value against Canada, with this agreement they can only do so to the equivalent value of the measure taken in this country. In other words, it is a big improvement on what we have at the present time.

Madam
Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate because some of the matters involved in the trade agreement have been grossly misunderstood. Certainly the Conservative Party seems unwilling to share its information with the people of Canada. It has been packaging a sales deal without discussing the real substance of the agreement.
We were told that many items would not be open for negotiation at the table, including culture and social services. We were asked to trust the Government and wait for the agreement. We did not think there would be any suggestion about any percentage. Traditionally, we have only had 3 per cent, but we now find that Canadian industries must compete internationally against huge corporations in the American market. They will only be subsidized with some funds to help them make proposals, but there is no guarantee for any part of their own market. That certainly interferes in our cultural industry.
We were also told that social programs would not be part of the negotiations in this trade deal. Lo and behold, we find that the administration of health care is part of the deal. Private corporations will be able to administer our non-profit public institutions.
A profit oriented health care system will cost the consumer more. Second, it reduces the delivery of service to the consumer. We must also compare non-profit health care delivery in Canada with that in the United States where health insurance is voluntary. We know that 40 per cent of the American population is not covered and that we have been able to provide health care services at less cost than the Americans. Yet the Government has opened the doors to the Americans for them to administer our health care system and our hospitals for a profit.
Ninety-seven per cent of Canadians treasure our health care delivery system and will not give it up easily. We will not accept this measure in the agreement, and the Government will recognize that as soon as it goes to the electorate for support.
We are also concerned about child care. There are some two million children under formal child care with standards of which we are not certain. For the first time in our history, the Government is providing public funds to private sector corporations in order to subsidize child care. This means that our tax dollars will go to help multinational child care facilities make a profit from child care.
Those who have been closely involved with child care over the years say that a lobby group has asked for a reduction in the standard of child care for such things as the number of staff, health conditions and space. The reason is that the current standards are too expensive and prevent the facilities from operating at a profit. The Government is saying, with its so-called national child care strategy, that it is willing to subsidize these multinationals with public funds.
We know that the trade agreement will require American companies to be treated the same as Canadian nationals. Canadians never thought their Government would go so far as to allow their children to become pawns in an agreement between two countries.
Never before has a trade agreement in the western world included services. Government officials, the Economic Council of Canada and others have consistently stated that they do not know the implications of trading services and have recommended that the Government not enter into such an agreement. Yet that is what the Government has done, and it is absolute nonsense to suggest that our sovereignty is intact.
I am sure the Minister was influenced by this trade deal and could no longer protect 15 per cent of our market for our film distribution. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. It concerns the extraordinary interference of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the independence of the refugee determination system over the case of Mr. Santokh Singh.
Following a unanimous ruling in favour of refugee status by the three distinguished members of the Refugee Status Advisory Committee, two former ambassadors to the Vatican and the UN, and one former head of the RSAC itself, the Secretary of State for External Affairs wrote two secret letters to the then Minister of Immigration, and on the basis of what seem to be purely personal, political, and diplomatic pressures, the Minister asked for and received an immediate reversal of this decision.
Can the Deputy Prime Minister inform this House and through this House give Canadians a rational explanation why an independent favourable decision based on advice from refugee experts was suddenly and politically overturned, and why the Department of External Affairs is allowed to dictate how refugee policy is run and operated in this country?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the ability of our health care services to be eroded by this trade agreement is very real. Since health care administration is now part of the agreement, we recognize the fact that it will not

May 16, 1988
Supply
take very long before people come into our system and say that the capability of making profit over quality of service delivery can be a priority.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Wrong!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: That's right!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
We do not need to have people from other countries coming in to make a profit out of that system. It is important that we do not allow that to happen. It is the slim edge of the wedge before all of a sudden our social service programs become eroded. That is of great concern.
With the increasing pressure to harmonize employment practices and social and economic programs with those of the United States, Canadian economic policy will be set by trade legislation rather than by domestic priorities and policies. The wonderful thing that has happened in Canada over the years has been that we have been very conscious of the fact that we wanted to set our own domestic priorities. Through that we have established a very strong social service network. We have also proven that when we deliver those types of services we do so efficiently and universally. More and more we are concerned that this type of deal will erode that very seriously.
I have in my hand some quotations of people who have looked forward to the trade agreement. The Canada West Foundation states that free trade between our two countries will inevitably lead to wages being equalized between Canada and the United States. It states that this will occur because a high cost producer will not be able to compete against a lower cost producer if goods are traded freely.
What is really being said is that if there are no minimum wages for labour and in some states in the U.S., let alone Canada, we know that the transfer flow of economy is taking place from the north to the south, then that will allow that type of abuse to take place. Certainly, what has happened in Canada is that we have recognized that we are a small population, a population that occupies a thin strip across the country. With that we have stood firm, strong and free. We have established a network that is very different from that in the United States.
We must recognize that with this agreement there are two visions of Canada. There is a vision of Canada about which many people-I would say the majority-say that social policy is important, that the weak and the vulnerable in the country need to be protected. That vision states that we recognize that there has to be a sharing of our resources if we are to have the type of civilized community that I think we have chosen to live in.
The other version of Canada is the version that states that the only economy that makes sense is a market-driven one so that profits can be maximized and so that people can be
exploited to the maximum. In this way we would become a North American fortress which says that we will maximize our profits in North America to the exclusion of the rest of the world, and ensure that we protect what we have here for the greatest profit. It is not a value system which Canadians have had over the years. It is not a value system that we want to have in the future.
When we talk about our sovereignty being eroded we are very serious about it. We know of the ability there is to take the whole military industrial complex and to have our country driven by what the United States foreign policy is all about as if to say that unless we have military jobs we will not have jobs at all. There is that type of talk going on. That is not what Canadians want. It certainly is not what our ancestors fought for over the years. It is not what we want to look forward to in the future for our children and our grandchildren.
When we talk about the trade agreement eroding our sovereignty, hurting our culture and interfering and weakening our social service network we recognize how important it is not to allow that to happen. This agreement must be stopped. It is important that it be stopped. I become quite upset when I hear people I have known for years who have attempted to protect the Canadian culture, now saying "We can compete anywhere in the United States or in Canada. We know that our writers, our artists, and many of our people could not compete if they had not been able to get some help nationally from Canada Council, from research, and those types of things".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: They still can.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: But the Government has talked about how they can still get it, but it has not identified what is a subsidy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: That is cultural. It is outside the agreement.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Culture is not outside the agreement. We saw last week what happened in the film industry. One year ago our Canadian industry was asking for 15 per cent of the market. It was not asking for great numbers, only a small piece of that market. What has the Government done? The Government has stated that that is far too much, that it will give some money to assist in making proposals internationally, and the film industry can compete with everybody else, but as far as the Canadian market is concerned, the industry has no right to have any exclusion in its own market. That is the type of agreement that we have in front of us.
When I hear people from the Government saying that the issue of culture is not on the table or that it is not affected, it certainly is affected. It means that we will continue not being able to see Canadian films. Those films can compete internationally, they have shown that. We have listened to the Government tell us that it has reduced tariffs over the years. We know that, and we have worked at making sure we do have freer trade among all nations. We know that that is a good
May 16, 1988

thing. However, this trade agreement is putting us into a North American fortress mentality. It is saying that we in North America must protect ourselves against everything else. That is not a vision that most Canadians have of this country.
We certainly see our economic development as involving multilateral trade, at getting a foothold in the Pacific Rim, and looking at the ability of trading our goods with people from other countries with massive populations. Perhaps with an enlightened Government we would not be tying all our aid to trade, but looking at what it is to be competitive in a multilateral way, and at the same time looking at the whole planet as part of the human family.
It is with great concern that we recognize that, if the agreement continues, the social service network will be threatened. We have seen what has been done with health care. It is on the table, and it is in the agreement. We know that the administration of the health care is there. We know that a subsidy has not been identified. We also know that unemployment insurance and health care are part of many of our labour agreements which could be seen by companies outside of Canada as a subsidy. The Government was afraid to identify what a subsidy was. We know that there have been complaints about our social services being part and parcel of our labour practices.
A well-known Vancouver entrepreneur, Jimmy Pattison, stated: "We are looking at manufacturing along the Mexican border and shipping into Canada. If we do that we will shut down plants in Canada and transfer to Mexico". That is lovely! Is that the type of Canada we want? That is not the type of Canada that we are looking for. The Jimmy Pattisons can go off to Mexico, but we do not want him to start shipping in here. What is happening is far too serious.
I heard the Government state that with this agreement we will end up with better consumer prices. It has been proven that a family will save approximately $50 a year on consumer prices. That is $50 a year to lose what we would lose. Over and above that, we would see the inability of consumers to purchase. If one does not have a job, it is very difficult to participate in consumerism.
The time has come when the Government has to come clean with the Canadian people. It has been packaging a sales package and stating that it is good for us. When specifics are asked for, one is told, "Trust us". In this day and age we have to learn that there has to be more than trust and more than a leap of faith.
We know what will happen to the data processing industry in Canada. We know how those jobs are flowing south of the border, and with the regulation gone of collecting the data in Canada, it looks upwards of 200,000 jobs per year. That study was produced by the Computer Association of Canada. When we look at the background in this agreement, we recognize that all we are getting back is a sales pitch and a trust. We know that our vision of Canada is too important to buy into a
Supply
sales pitch without any substantive foundation. It is high time that the whole trade agreement was eroded.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Does Annex 1408 ring a bell with the Hon. Member? The provision of day care is exempt from the agreement. Does the Hon. Member understand Annex 1408? She obviously has not read or understood the agreement.
The Hon. Member further stated that Canada cannot review foreign investment under the deal. We can. It means that we can review the top 500 Canadian companies. To make the statement that Canada cannot review foreign investment is absolutely false.
The Hon. Member also stated that Canada will only trade with the United States. The Hon. Member obviously does not understand that the spin-off from this agreement, when Canadian companies grow in economy of scale, it will make them more productive and more competitive on the world market. That is what this whole thing is all about. Until the NDP understand that, and understand how business operates, and how when production is expanded there is economy of scale and we can compete better in the world, only then will the NDP understand the importance of international trade in all areas of the world to Canada and to our economy. Thirty per cent of what we produce is exported. We rely on trade more than any other country, with the exception of Germany. It is so important to our economy. For the New Democratic Party to make totally false statements without substantiation is a disservice to the Canadian public.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
I think it is about time that the Government understood, and certainly the Hon. Member recognized that, that when we start to put all our eggs in one basket and trade with only one major trading partner, we reduce our ability for multinational trading. One does not have to be overly intelligent to figure that out.
We must also recognize that, for the first time, the Government has allowed public dollars to go into private profit-

May 16, 1988
Supply
making day care delivery. As multinationals come in, they will be able to get that type of subsidy from the Canadian Government. That is wrong. That is the type of thing that makes a ploy of Canadian children. The Government must start to recognize what are the true needs in this country. One of the true needs is the delivery of quality care service to our children. We know that there are 2 million children in informal care, and some of it is pretty disastrous. I think if we were really committed to that notion we would not be looking at trying to find ways for people to make a profit and saying that we will put public dollars into profit-making centres.
We have to recognize that much child care now is under the aegis of multinational companies. When those companies come into Canada they will be treated as national companies, and there are the kinds of things that start to erode our social services system. The Hon. Member, with good intention, is defending an indefensible kind of accord. My sympathy is with him. I recognize that he probably does mean well, but when you get an agreement like this, which really gives the country away and invites the Americans to come into Canada under their terms not ours, that is pretty hard to defend. I can understand why outrageous statements are being made.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my short answer is that the Canadian Government has already set the stage for that by allowing the multinationals to come into child care.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when we look at this trade deal there is a lot of talk about competition. Canadians are fully capable of competing. We are able to compete when we work and when we have the advantage of Canadian resources and the advantage of Canadian programs. This deal seems to open the door for Americans to come here and have access to our resources and we will not have the advantage of our own resources. The Americans will continue to have the advantages of their resources and of a huge financial pool. They will continue to have the resources of established markets and brands in those markets. We will have to compete with them after we have given away our competitive edge. The long-term effect is that Canadian companies, in an attempt to compete, will have to compete by cutting the standards of Canadian workers to the standards of workers in American states where
there are right-to-work laws and where there are no minimum wages.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: No, that is phoney.

speechtext:
The Hon. Member says it is phoney. I challenge him to show how it is phoney. Perhaps he can speak later on.
Will my colleague comment on this whole question of competition and the ability of Canadians to compete if they are given half a chance and the ability of Canadians to compete if the whole competitive edge for Canada has been wiped out by this trade deal?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for his question. Many of us are becoming very tired listening to the propaganda coming from the government side, saying those who are against this deal really are afraid to let Canadians compete. I think it is very clear how well we have competed internationally up until now. Certainly in the communications technology field we have shown how well we can do, and we constantly hear how well Canadian companies are doing now. We know that the United States has a trade deficit with Canada. With all of that, certainly Canadian companies are doing well and Canadians workers are doing well. We have confidence in their competition.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: It is the status quo.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
It is not the status quo. This country has never lived in the status quo. Anybody knows that the status quo is suffocation. We know that unless you generate, initiate and support creativity you shrivel up and die.
We are looking for, and certainly what New Democrats want to see, is an economy that is bubbling and a strong economy with Canadian direction in it that will be very competitive in the world. That is the situation we are starting into right now. This deal will tie us very much into large companies. Decisions will be made by boards of directors in head offices south of the border. We will not have the ability to have the same kind of competitive edge that we have now, and I think it is important that people understand that. I understand my colleague's frustration at trying to defend an indefensible deal.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in today's debate.
Since the beginning of our term in September 1984, our Government has always stressed the fact that Canadian women should enjoy their fair share of the results of our efforts to expand the economy.
Madam Speaker, the New Democratic Party should be cheering the Government on today instead of tabling motions
May 16, 1988

condemning the Government for signing a free trade agreement with the Americans.
Madam Speaker, I intend to quote just a few figures to show that the Conservative Government has definitely kept, I would say ... 90 per cent of its promises.
We created nearly 1,223,000 jobs, of which 82 per cent are full-time jobs, and 679,000 of those full-time jobs are held by women.
The Opposition Parties talk about unemployment and the unemployment rate. Madam Speaker, three and half years ago this Government came to power, and although I agree that more remains to be done, I think we should realize that the unemployment rate, which was 11.7 per cent in September 1984, dropped to 7.7 per cent in April 1988. They should be applauding, because this is indeed a real accomplishment. And what about interest rates that have gone down enormously, and today, and I see this in my own riding of Argenteuil- Papineau, we are enjoying economic growth as never before. We have never had so many construction starts, for instance. Everybody knows that when the construction industry is in good shape, the economy is in good shape. I see that in my riding!
Reducing the deficit has also been a very important achievement. As for real economic growth, Canada has the best record of all members of the OECD. Isn't that something to applaud, Madam Speaker?
Fewer Canadians are living at the poverty line, and I agree we cannot afford to be complacent about our achievements because much remains to be done, but we have made some headway.
Foreign investment has doubled since 1984. I referred earlier to the construction industry, consumer spending, price stability and the increase in farm income.
Madam Speaker, I simply want to say today that as far as I am concerned, Canadian women have everything to gain from the Agreement because they will get a substantial share of the opportunities and advantages arising from the free trade agreement.
On May 5, the Minister responsible for the Status of Women (Mrs. McDougall) released a report on free trade and women, which assesses the impact of the agreement on Canadian women. Her conclusion was clear. She said that free trade will mean better job opportunities for women.
Madam Speaker, I fail to understand why, for instance, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, in Ottawa today for its annual lobby meeting, is against the Agreement. They are here to tell us about their objectives, I say to them that women should support the agreement, and all eminent experts who have examined the agreement and its various sections and the impact on women, say that many new jobs created as a result of the agreement will be in the service industry. Canadian women are in a very good position to take
Supply
advantage of this expansion, because they already represent more than half the work force in the service industry in this country. In fact, 84 per cent of Canadian women working outside the home are employed in this industry.
With free trade, existing companies will grow to take advantage of the more secure access to the American market. Increased trade and greater demand for consumer goods will lead to the creation of new businesses.
Madam Speaker, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs also conducted a study on the impact of free trade on consumers. The largest consumers of goods and services in our society are women. They do the shopping for the children, for groceries and so on. So women consumers themselves will benefit from lower prices, because with increased trade, there will be more products and prices will keep going down. 1 am sure, Madam Speaker, that when free trade will be fully implemented, Canadian women consumers will be even happier to see their purchasing power greatly increased.
The paper also looks at the impact of the agreement on women working in the manufacturing sector. Under free trade, according to Department of Finance estimates, manufacturing production in Canada could rise by 10 per cent.
The abolition of customs duties, the lowering of non-tariff barriers and the increased security of access to the American market are all factors that will help Canadian manufacturers improve their efficiency and achieve economies of scale. With lower input costs, these manufacturers will be able to become more competitive. More efficient, more competitive companies will be able to create more and better jobs for Canadians, men and women.
Madam Speaker, once again, as this document points out, the female work force in manufacturing is divided among the various industries of this sector. Thus these working women are in a good position to reap the benefits this sector will enjoy after the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement takes effect.
Certainly, Madam Speaker, and we do not deny it, some adjustments will be necessary. But I do not think they will be major. In fact, it is expected that the dislocation will largely be offset by the overall growth in trade and the employment opportunities created by free trade. In the past, working women have had to make many such adjustments and they have come through them well. God knows, Madam Speaker, as you do, that women come through all right everyv/here!
Furthermore, the changes required by free trade will be gradual, since a ten-year transition period is provided in the Agreement.
There has been much talk of adjusting workers to free trade. Through programs such as the Job Strategy, and the Industry Adjustment Program, we are now in a position to respond to situations where women could need training or adjustment, or are in an industry or community undergoing changes of some kind.

May 16, 1988
Supply
We are hopeful that our programs are adequate to meet the adjustment needs deriving from free trade, but in order to ensure the fastest and most efficient response we have set up an adjustment advisory council including representatives from business, labour, consumers' associations and education institutions, to assess our programs and ensure that we are in a position to adequately respond to any new situation. Just like the Hon. Member from the New Democratic Party, I can state, Madam Speaker, that as a Government Member in this House, I am concerned with and especially interested in the advancement of women in our society, and I can state that on this side of the House, all of us women Members, including you, Madam Speaker, have looked at the free trade agreement from top to bottom to ensure that the free trade agreement in no way hinders the advancement or even the jobs of women.
Madam Speaker, I can assure my women constituents that I have a special interest in that matter, and I can assure them today that, despite what the New Democratic Party might suggest, women are not victimized by the free trade agreement, quite the opposite. We can expect there will be a larger number of non-traditional job opportunities in primary industry for women. The new markets opened to small businesses are another area of interest to women, because the latter are playing an increasing role in Canadian small businesses.
Earlier, Madam Speaker, I referred to the Action Committee on the Status of Women, and their suggestion that Canadian women oppose free trade made me wonder, because I know a number of women in the small and medium-business sector who support and welcome free trade.
So, when the Canadian Action Committee suggests that women oppose it, I tend to wonder because women own more than one third of Canadian small businesses. Free trade will bring to these entrepreneurs both new business opportunities and greater access to the huge American market.
The free trade agreement also is good news for women farmers, since women have an essential role in Canadian farming, Madam Speaker. They account for 30 per cent of farm labour in this country. In co-operation with their husbands, they operate a very large majority of family farms. It is a well-known fact, Madam Speaker, that without women participation in agriculture, family farms would not be what they are today. Again, family farms account for 99 per cent of Canadian farm operations.
In addition, 23,000 women operate their own farms. The free trade agreement features a series of important measures which will give Canadians more generous and more secure conditions to export agricultural products to the huge American market. Canadian producers, men and women alike, will gain real benefits. Plentiful Canadian agricultural and food products, meats, grains, oil-producing seeds and potatoes will be in a position to compete fairly with American products on the U.S. market.
Madam Speaker, I can tell you that if the free trade agreement were in effect right now the Notre-Dame-de-la-Paix potato growers who have to cope with overproduction and all sorts of problems would find a secure market and they probably would not be experiencing the difficulties they have now.
The agreement does not restrict the right of the federal and provincial Governments to establish and maintain programs designed to protect and stabilize agricultural income. Free trade will not affect the future of wheat, dairy, chicken and egg marketing boards, nor Canada's right to set up new marketing boards. This sector will not be affected. I can say that because there are ongoing negotiations on potatoes, and I am sure that with the free trade agreement we would still be able to create a potato marketing board. Canadian farmers can indeed look forward to the day free trade does become a fact of life. Much the same thing can be said about Canadian consumers, for they too will benefit from more generous conditions with respect to agricultural trade between Canada and the United States.
As consumers, Canadian women-I said this earlier-take a special interest in the impact of the free trade agreement on prices, if only because a larger share of their personal or family income goes for basic expenses such as those for food, clothing, and housing. Madam Speaker, you know how much money women have to spend on clothes. Fashion being what it is these days, we like our shoes to match the colour of our outfits. As consumers, we need access to better products in a wider market, but at more reasonable prices, of course.
The Canada-U.S. trade agreement will do away with tariff barriers which inflate prices and restrict the consumer's choice. It will make prices more competitive, widen the selection of goods and services, and increase the quality of products.
It is estimated that tariff elimination will reduce the cost of American products by 5 per cent. After the Agreement comes into effect, the price of Canadian products should equally fall by 3 per cent during the transition period. That reduction will be achieved by a lower cost of inputs and an increased efficiency resulting from the economies of scale.
Madam Speaker, it means that a family-the Hon. Member for Hamilton-East finds that funny-would save between $300 and $800 each year and be able to buy more products. The document released on May 5 gives an estimate of the savings that can be made by consumers in general and four different groups of women in particular. This is an important point because Canadian women play a significant role in the support of families.
One last word, madam Speaker. Canadians are proud and rightly so of their social security system. Many of the programs which make it up have already been implemented to meet the needs identified by women and their organizations. The Agreement in no way affects the basic system, nor does it preclude the establishment of new programs. In fact, the
May 16, 1988

economic growth which will flow from free trade will strengh-en the financial foundation of our social programs.
Again I do not understand the obstinate and erroneous contention of the opposition Parties that the Free Trade Agreement will jeopardize our social programs. How inconceivable, how incomprehensible for members of this House to make such assertions! The Free Trade Agreement is an economic agreement, no more no less. We are not relinquishing our sovereignty. On the contrary, we are exercising it since, by concluding this Agreement, we will improve our position vis-a-vis the United States and other countries. For women, this vision of the future would appear as a culmination of the efforts of many of us to improve our life and hppefully of other women's. Change is not a bad thing when it implies an improvement. For women, free trade will open up a new range of opportunities. To cling to the past inevitably leads to failure. Women know something about that.
Madam Speaker, I will conclude by saying that I am most proud to be part of a Government which has looked to the future instead of gazing at the past, which was able to sit down and negotiate an agreement. As the Prime Minister has said, this agreement is by no means perfect, but it allows us to face the future more optimistically and without the threat of protectionist measures, to react, in case of an emergency, as a unified country, not as provinces and regions, since the agreement will benefit all of Canada. That is why I think the opposition parties should applaud the government and try to cooperate in improving the agreement instead of saying that they will tear it up. Madam Speaker, those are the attitudes of people who cling to the past and who are not looking into the future. In conclusion, the Progressive Conservative Party looks into the future determined to pass on to our children the same kind of economy we have enjoyed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member just stated that harmonizing would only start with standards concerning goods that are imported into Canada. How come then the Committee on Subsidies will be sitting for the next five or seven years?

I simply want to remind her that anyone who is interested in bilateral trade should look at what is happening in other countries. I think we should look at what happened in Europe and in New Zealand and Australia. From what I gathered upon reading the documentation, Madam Speaker, before these agreements were ratified the socialist parties and the unions were against the free trade agreement that now exists within the European Economic Community. Today, the same organizations, and I hope the New Democrats are listening, view with some embarrassment their erstwhile objections to an agreement that has enhanced the economies of the Common Market countries, while New Zealand has benefited enormously under the free trade agreement signed with Australia.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am delighted the Hon. Member asked us to look at the situation in Europe. She should have known that in Europe, they started with a trade agreement and now they are harmonizing their social programs, including retirement age. For instance, we know that in Italy, the retirement age for women was lower than for men, but that is now changing. Member take this particular instance as an example of an economic agreement, when we know that in Europe, what they are doing is social harmonizing of social programs?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, trying to compare the European Economic Community with Canada and the United States is like comparing apples and oranges.
Madam Speaker, those discussions were held with the Council of the European Economic Community. That does not mean that Canada will reach the same conclusion; I hope not. Look, when she points out that European countries are harmonizing their programs, that is their business. As far as we are concerned, we are in North America, a completely different situation. There is just no comparison. In Europe, you can travel from one country to another in an hour or two, but we know how big Canada is. There is no comparison whatever. We have provinces, each with its own jurisdiction.
So, Madam Speaker, this issue, this statement is not very relevant.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the Member now states that there is no relationship between this deal and the European community because only a few short moments ago the Member herself said: "Look to the European community to see what kind of a terrific deal they have signed". If you examine the history of the European community, you will find that first comes an economic deal and then comes the so-called harmonization of social policy. The Government time and again claims that harmonization has no bearing whatsoever on this trade deal, but it will
devastate the social safety net we have established in this country and the benefits and protections which we have provided to women through such things as pregnancy benefits.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Cheap shot.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
The Member says "cheap shot". I do not think it is a cheap shot to talk about what is going to happen with the future of the country. In the course of harmonization over the next five to seven years the leaders of our country, who have been selling us down the drain for the last four years, will get together with American leaders to try to develop a so-called check list of what constitutes an unfair subsidy. Do government Members think that it is our social policy and our laws that will harmonize with the Americans? Do the Members think they will accept pregnancy benefits similar to those which we have in Canada and unemployment insurance such as we have? No, we will harmonize to their programs.
I would like to provide a check list of what we can expect under the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal which inherently involves the harmonization of social programs because "harmonization" is the hidden watchword, the hidden buzz word, the ticking time bomb in this deal that will change the very fabric and face of a country which we have fought so hard to build.
The United States has yet to ratify the International Labour Organization Convention of 1975 which sets standards for all women workers. Section 103 of the ILO Code states that there must be a minimum leave period of 12 weeks for pregnant women, protection against dismissal, and a minimum standard that cash benefits during pregnancy leave be sufficient for the full and healthy maintenance of the child. These are the standards which the U.S. has refused to sign. They have refused to sign because in their jurisdiction the protection of pregnant women simply does not exist.
The social safety net of unemployment insurance for unemployed workers in that country falls far short of even respecting the poverty level. In fact, there are only five states in the United States which provide publicly paid pregnancy leave for women. If a woman happens to have a child in those states she can leave work for six to eight weeks. The stellar states include California, Hawaii, New Jersey, New York and Rhode Island. In 45 other states there is no public law providing any kind of financial assistance for women who leave the job during a period of pregnancy.
