speechtext: All Hon. Members will have the opportunity to debate. It is very difficult for the Speaker to hear what the Member who has the floor is saying when there is such very loud talking across the floor. The Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) has the floor.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Thank you, Madam Speaker. The net result of the lack of national social policy which currently exists in the United States is that only 40 per cent of working women in the United States are entitled to any paid maternity, including from private companies, of at least six weeks duration. I do not think we want to see such a program here.
Earlier today, during Question Period, we heard the Minister who is supposed to be responsible for the Status of Women say that this trade deal has no effect on women and no effect on the textile industry because our threat is from the Third World countries, pays d'outre-mer.
Does the Government recognize that textile workers in the southern sun belt states of the United States pose a real threat to competition in Canada? Would we like our minimum wage laws harmonized with American minimum wage laws? Nine American states have no minimum wage whatsoever. Twelve states have a minimum wage under $3 U.S. The minimum wage in Texas is $1.40 an hour. The Government has the gall to say that this will have no effect whatsoever in the trade deal which basically says that Canadians and Americans are supposed to be able to compete on an equal basis. I do not want my constituents working at Coppley, Noyes & Randall, a clothing factory, to have to work for the equivalent of $1.40 U.S.
The harmonization process which will take place as a result of this deal will not only see devastation in social programs and in the national health care system which Canadians hold very dear, but will also see a downward pressure on wage scales because we are supposed to compete with states which have right- to-work laws which abolish the right of the union to automatic dues check-off, that do not believe in minimum wages, and which, frankly, have gone a different route in terms of national economy and national social structure and social policy.
Let us look at the issue of health care. The Parliamentary Secretary guffaws and chortles over there. It was not I who said before the travelling trade committee in Vancouver that medicare would be under threat as a result of this deal. It was the President of the B.C. Council on National Issues. That group came before the committee and said that it is okay that
Supply
this deal will threaten medicare because they have to become more competitive.
With regard to the harmonization of our health care system with the United States, let us look at the auto worker in Canada. The wage package portion of an auto worker's salary in Canada, which includes premiums for health, accident, dental, vision, and life insurance, is equivalent to approximately $2,800 Canadian. The same firm in the United States, because of the absence of a national health care plan, pays about $8,900 Canadian per worker in annual premiums for health, accident, dental, vision and life insurance. What happens, for purposes of discussion, if once this infamous trade deal is set in motion American auto makers come to the table and say that they think the medicare system in Canada is an unfair subsidy because their employers have to pay $8,900 per worker whereas in Canada they only pay $2,800?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Why haven't they done it then?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
The Member asks why they haven't done it. They did it. They did it with the shakes and shingles and they did it with ground-fish. With regard to shakes and shingles, a 1983 complaint against Canada was struck down and in 1987 a complaint was upheld. The same thing could happen in the area of unemployment insurance. The same thing could happen in the area of health care.
Let us look at what is available for Americans in the area of medical insurance. A quarter of American women of child bearing age have no medical insurance whatsoever. America's infant mortality rate is 40 per cent higher than Canada's. Is that the direction in which we want our social programs to go? Do we want to see an increase in infant mortality which is directly related to inaccessibility to a universal health care system such as we have developed in this country?
On top of 47 million Americans who have no medical coverage whatsoever, 15 million have inadequate coverage. The American Medicaid program is actually targeted to the lower half of people living below the poverty line. One must be in the bottom half of those living below the poverty line in order to be eligible for Medicaid.
A recent study from the auto workers shows that those people who were hardest hit, unemployed workers, are the ones who dropped off from medical coverage. Only 30 per cent of unemployed American workers had any health insurance at all.
We know that Annex 1408 of the trade agreement identifies health care facilities management services as a sector in which we are extending national treatment. If health care is not under discussion, why does Annex 1408 of the trade agreement open the door for an influx of private sector, profit oriented companies to come into Canada to establish their own systems like we have seen with American Humana Corporation. Is that the kind of health care system we want for our country?

May 16, 1988
Supply

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: What does that have to do with the trade agreement?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Again the question is asked: "What does that have to do with the trade agreement"? The trade agreement calls for a harmonization of our laws. When the European Common Market first set up a trade agreement, the natural sequence of a trade agreement was social benefit harmonization. That is why a subsidy committee was set up. Over the next five to seven years it will sit down and play Russian roulette with these social programs and the benefits and guarantees that have been given to working men and women in this country.
I, for one, do not trust the statement from a Government and a Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who first came into office saying senior citizens' pensions will not be touched. The same Government and the same Prime Minister is saying that social programs will not be touched.
Let us talk about the food sector industry. A short time ago I received a letter from the plant manager of an American multinational in my community known as Procter and Gamble. The plant manager wrote a letter saying that we should be supporting this wonderful trade deal. However, he did not include a memorandum which had been circulated to the Liberal trade committee. It is a private letter from the Vice-President of McCain Foods, who just happens to be a good Conservative.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: McCain kept loaning his plane to Pierre all the time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
I am sorry that the Government is not aware of the facts surrounding this letter. I will spend a few moments reading parts of it into the record. It states: "Dear Miss Carney: I am writing to you as a member of the agriculture SAGIT and as a hard core Tory..." The letter is from Archie McLean, who was with McCain Foods. This hard core Tory points out how this trade deal will not only devastate the dairy, poultry or feather, horticulture, beer and wine industries, it will reek devastation upon the food processing industry across this country. He also implies in the letter that one of the reasons that most corporations in Canada have not spoken out against the deal is because most of them are 100 per cent U.S. owned.
Let me run through the table. They include Procter and Gamble. I will say right now to those workers in my riding who would like to know whether they can buy matching shoes and dresses, in reference to comments made by the Member who spoke previously, that they will not be able to buy matching shoes and dresses if they do not have jobs. Procter and Gamble in my community will have very little lifetime left in Canada if this trade deal goes through. It has 100 per cent U.S. ownership, with annual sales in Canada of S939 million.
Other companies include Nabisco Brands with 80 per cent U.S. ownership; Kraft, 100 per cent U.S. owned; General Foods, 100 per cent U.S. owned; Coca Cola, 100 per cent U.S.
owned; Beatrice International, 100 per cent U.S. owned. Do Members really believe these companies are fighting for the jobs of Canadians?
This same vice-president of McCain Foods stated clearly that the President of Heinz has already told him they have plans to move their plant production to the United States if this trade deal goes through. Naturally, they are not standing up one by one to decry this deal, because they are owned by American multinationals.
Only three companies in this sector are majority Canadian owned. They are B.C. Tree Fruits, McCain Foods Canada and Canberra Foods. The vast majority of the food processing industry in Canada is owned by Americans.
It is like Cameo in my community, a company which makes refrigerators. Everyone believes that they will be able to buy cheap refrigerators once this deal goes through. However, I have spoken to officials with Cameo Corporation who say that if this deal goes through, there will be excess capacity in American manufacturing plants that can service and sell a refrigerator to every Canadian with some left over. Cameo will be on the chopping block as well.
The Government says that there will be some minor adjustments as a result of this deal. The Finance Department figures which came out last summer and allegedly gave us a sector by sector breakdown of what we could expect in terms of winners and losers were an absolute farce. They could not indicate in absolute numbers what industries would be on top and what industries would falter. I know that in my community the steel industry is supposed to be a winner. However, the Canadian steel producers stated categorically to the trade committee, that they had no intention of selling more steel in the U.S. market.
The status of the Canadian dollar is also a hidden time bomb. Early last week, we had breakfast with the Canadian Foundries Association, who are terrified about the increase in value of the Canadian dollar. As it continues to increase, probably as a result of some back room deal signed between Americans and Canadians in the same way they allowed the drug Bill to go through-the competitive edge upon which the original premise of the deal was based is eroded. The steel producers themselves will say that an 80-cent dollar will wreak havoc on what is now a competitive industry.
While these are many questions, the most important one concerns the ultimate direction of our country. Government Members chortle and say this has nothing to do with social programs. The key watchword is harmonization. Will this committee sit down over the next five to seven years and bargain away our national health care system? Will it bargain away any expansion of that system with something like parental leave for fathers, or ruin any potential plan for an increase in a national child care delivery program? Will it say that affirmative action programs and regional development programs are subsidy oriented and therefore cannot be permitted? Are we as Canadians willing to abdicate our right
May 16, 1988

to develop our own future to some committee that will sit down over the next five to seven years and wipe out all the gains we have made in establishing a separate and different identity?
The Government Members consistently kowtow to their American neighbours. They accuse us of being anti-American. I certainly do not categorize myself as anti-American. However, I believe that as a country we have determined a future course which is different from the Americans. I do not want to see an infant mortality rate 40 per cent higher than what we have now in Canada. I do not want to see legislation that does not protect pregnant women, so that they can get kicked out of their jobs merely because they got pregnant. If we move to harmonize, that is the direction in which we will go. That is why it is so important that we fight tooth and nail to prevent this Bill from ever becoming the law of the land.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps). I would like to ask her a few questions. She said there is a term in the agreement that talks about harmonization of laws. The problem, in my view, is that in our system of Government, whatever the Government proposes, with very few exceptions, opposition Members have to oppose it as if their lives depended on it. That, in my view, explains a good deal of the absolutely empty rhetoric we are hearing today from the opposition Parties.
Would the Member tell the House where in the agreement the expression "harmonization of laws" appears? Where in the agreement does the expression "harmonization of social programs" appear? In my respectful submission, the Member should know, if she does not, that there is nothing in the agreement that says that social programs shall be harmonized. For example, Governor Dukakis of Massachusetts, as the Member probably knows, is arguing for a health care plan similar to the one we have in Canada. If Governor Dukakis is elected, presumably the United States will have a health care plan along the lines of our health care plan.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Without free trade.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Without free trade, of course. I submit respectfully that the Hon. Member is not arguing on the merits of the agreement. What members of the Opposition are doing is what President Lincoln once said about an opposing attorney: "If you do not have a good case, abuse the plaintiffs attorney". Opposition Members are not talking about the merits of the agreement. They are simply trying to scaremonger along the lines my journalist friend, David Crane, has been doing.
When the Member talks about her extreme affection for Americans, I recall an interview a couple of years ago in which the Member and I were both interviewed by someone from the Los Angles Times. The reporter found it most amusing that the Member made exactly the same point and then in the next four paragraphs of the interview, she did nothing but attack
Supply
the United States as she has been doing here in the Chamber. I put it to her that it rings a little bit hollow to say she has extreme affection for Americans, talking about her husband's country of origin, when she in fact, from everything I have ever read the Member saying, has nothing but contempt for the United States. I put it to the Hon. Member that if we had Peruvians or Bolivians living there, or anyone else on earth, the Member and the New Democratic Party would have quite a different view. The reality is that there are 23 industrial democracies in the world today. If this agreement goes ahead, as I very much hope it will, only one of them, Japan, will not be a member of a trading agreement.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by addressing the Hon. Member's last point first. My father-in-law will be very surprised to learn when he comes up for a visit that I hold Americans in contempt. Perhaps it is because I have spent some time in my husband's home State of Florida that I have a little concern about what we are getting into with the so-called free trade agreement. Almost every time I go there to visit my in-laws, I hear about someone killing themselves because they cannot afford to face the financial burden of an accident. The last time I was in Florida, there was a double murder suicide. A woman's young son had injured himself in a motorcycle accident and had ended up a quadriplegic. The drain on the family's economy in dealing with that young man who was very seriously debilitated was such that the family had been driven into bankruptcy. They had lost everything they owned. The woman felt the only honourable way out was to kill herself and her son.
Perhaps I feel this way because I have looked at some of the legislation there which does not protect working women or ordinary working people. We have a system here which has developed in a different way. Yes, it has more government involvement. Unlike the Conservatives, I am not radically opposed to government involvement at any cost. I feel that we as a society have developed programs to support the regions and minorities in a way that has not been the case in the United States. I like our way of life. I do not want to trade it for what I see south of the border however much I may admire and respect and have friendships with the people south of the border.
I am a Canadian. I think my leader said it best when he said: "We may pay a little more to put chicken on the table in Canada". Yes, we do pay a little more because we have marketing boards which feel that farmers are entitled to an honest living and should not be simply at the mercy of the rise and fall of the market-place", as we can see with the devastation of the family farm in the United States. I do not begrudge it because, as a Canadian, I feel it is a price worth paying.
Second, on the issue of harmonization, if the Hon. Member does not believe me, I ask that he consider a statement by Health and Welfare Canada. There was an assessment done by the Canadian Council on Social Development which basically deals with the question of subsidies and the fact that since

May 16, 1988
Supply
there is currently no definition of "subsidy" in the agreement, the next five years to seven years will tell the tale as to what happens to social programs. I ask Canadians if they think that when we are sitting at the table with American negotiators, negotiating what constitutes an unfair subsidy, our subsidies and our programs will win out, or will the American programs win out? I tend to think we will be sinking to the lowest common denominator in terms of public programs. That is why I do not want the deal to go through.
Once the agreement is implemented, according to the Canadian Council of Social Development, Canadians could face countervail after we have reduced our tariffs. This is no idle threat, since the Trade Bill before the U.S. Congress includes a very broad definition of subsidies and since U.S. negotiators have already indicated that Canadian social programs could be considered subsidies. These are not my words. These are the words of a bulletin issued by Health and Welfare Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the comments of the Hon. Member and I wonder if I might ask a question. In one of her comments the Hon. Member referred to the fact that one of the consequences of a freer trade agreement, say, the European example, was social benefits, harmonization. I think those were her words. I would like to quote the C. D. Howe Institute study of September of 1987. It talked about the lessons of the European Economic Community for freer trade between Canada and the United States. In the conclusion it was stated:
The European experience suggests, and theoretical considerations confirm, that free trade is compatible with an amazing degree of diversity. In fact, one only has to look within federal states to see just how much diversity survives after decades, if not centuries, of economic unity. The harmonization of laws is simply not necessary. Sweden can retain its extensive social welfare system- and the high level of taxation that goes with it; Switzerland can remain at the other end of this spectrum, with a maximum of self-help and low levels of taxation; Austria can run its economy on largely state-owned lines; Finland can retain its special relationship with the Soviet Union.
Here we have some of these countries which are in the European Free Trade Association that trade with the European Common Market and, according to the conclusion of the C. D. Howe Institute, the harmonization of laws is simply not necessary. Yet the Hon. Member suggested that harmonization has to follow, that it is a natural consequence. Why then has it not occurred in Europe? Why is it that the C. D. Howe Institute, in looking at the lessons of Europe and at the European Free Trade Association and its association with the European Common Market, suggests the contrary?
From 1981 to 1984, which is the last year for which I have the figures available for the amount of money we put into our health care program, compared to what the Americans put in as a percentage of their GNP, the Americans on average put in 10.4 per cent. We put in 8.6 per cent. Yet we have a comprehensive universal scheme. Therefore, if we can service all Canadians, and we can do so cheaper than the Americans, then on whom is the pressure, them or us? I would like the Hon. Member to comment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, first, obviously, the Hon. Member does not know what the European community is since three of the countries he mentioned are not even in the European community.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: I said three trade associations.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
I said the European community. It does not include Finland, Austria and Switzerland. If the Hon. Member is talking about FTAC countries, that is one thing, but if the Hon. Member is talking about countries in the European community, which is what I referred to, then the Hon. Member is talking about countries that are moving toward a harmonization of their social programs. Obviously, the Hon. Member is not aware of the objective of 1992.
I will give Members of the House a very specific example of how harmonization of social programs is currently in effect in Europe, and moving into effect. In Italy, a country from which many of my constituents originally came, until this point in time there was a retirement program which is different for men and women. The mandatory retirement age for women in Italy is 55, while it is 60 for men. The reason that was originally instituted was to recognize that during the years of childbirth women undergo physical strain which means that they should be given a different retirement age.
Under the harmonization of social programs, which is currently being carried out in the European community, Italy has been advised to change its retirement age. I suspect that when Italy moves to revise it, it will not say to all men: "You can now retire at age 55". It will be moved upward. The age of retirement for all women in Italy is being changed, not because of a social policy change in the Italian Government but because of a directive from the European community which is moving to harmonize social programs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. As a point of clarification, the countries named in the C. D. Howe study at which I was looking concerns countries outside the European Common Market that have trading relationships with the European Common Market. It is that study which I quoted.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Resuming debate with the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have been listening to the debate with great interest today. I welcome the opportunity to talk about the free trade agreement and to participate in the debate on the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald). I take the Hon. Member's motion seriously, even though it is seriously flawed. The motion condemns the Government for "voluntarily relinquishing political sovereignty in the 'trade' deal".
May 16, 1988

I submit that any international agreement, any contract between two parties, imposes limits on the scope of the action of those parties. In 1974, the Liberals signed an agreement with the International Energy Agency of which Canada is a member, along with our 25 partners in that agency. That agreement stated that in a time of oil shortage throughout the world these 26 countries would share their resources equally. At that particular time in signing that agreement, an agreement with which I agree since I feel it makes sense, we gave up some of our sovereignty. We agreed to share our energy resources with our 25 partners in the International Energy Agency. I submit that any contract imposes limits on the freedom of individuals, just as international agreements or treaties for as long as they are in force impose limits on the sovereignty of countries.
When Canada helped to establish the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade some 40 years ago, it agreed to abide by the rules and regulations defined in that agreement. That was our commitment to our 96 partners now in GATT. The GATT thus prevents us from fully exercising our sovereignty in trade matters. We saw that recently in the decisions handed down by a couple of GATT panels, one which dealt with the discriminatory pricing of liquor and wines and the other which dealt with fish and how it is handled on the west coast of Canada. There are certain rules that we have to follow. In following those rules we give up a little bit of our sovereignty. But we do that with any agreement that is signed.
I suggest from reading the Hon. Member's motion that she is suggesting that we never sign international agreements because they limit some freedom to exercise sovereignty. Surely that is not what my friend, the former Mayor of Ottawa, and now the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar), was saying in her remarks when she was speaking to this motion. We only accept limits on our sovereignty in exchange for limits on the sovereignty of others.
I have been involved in the free trade agreement very closely for the last couple of years. It is interesting to hear some of the arguments put forward in the United States that that country has given up some of its sovereignty. Americans have complained to their elected representatives that they have given up some of their sovereignty in signing this agreement with Canada. That is right. We both give and we both take. That is what an international agreement is all about. That is what any agreement is all about.
The sovereignty debate on this matter is a red herring. Let us go beyond that. I believe that the Hon. Member's concern centres on the ability of all levels of Government in Canada to establish programs or plans related to such matters as day care, auto insurance and cultural industries.
Let us deal firstly with day care. The provision of day care is exempt from the agreement. It does not appear in the list of the services specified in Article 1408 of the agreement. I want to remind the Hon. Member that it was this Government, after the free trade agreement was signed, that introduced a
Supply
national day care policy. This is something which mothers and fathers have been seeking for 20 years. We announced our national day care policy shortly after the legal text between Canada and the United States was signed and made public. But nothing in this agreement prevented us from having such a program, and the Hon. Member knows that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Your day care program feeds right into it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
We can debate the benefits of the day care program another time. All I am saying is that we have every right to introduce social programs that we want.
Let me deal now with the cultural industries. Article 2005 specifically exempts cultural industries from the agreement. Article 2012 defines what is meant by a cultural industry. I wish to read this into the record so that people will know what we are talking about. Under Article 2012 it states:
a)	the publication, distribution, or sale of books, magazines, periodicals, or newspapers in print or machine readable form but not including the sole activity of printing or typesetting any of the foregoing,
b)	the production, distribution, sale or exhibition of film or video recordings,
c)	the production, distribution, sale or exhibition of audio or video music recordings,
d)	the publication, distribution, or sale of music in print or machine readable form, or
e)	radio communication in which the transmissions are intended for direct reception by the general public, and all radio, television and cable television broadcasting undertakings and all satellite programming and broadcast network services;
Could the agreement be any more explicit? Could the list of cultural industries be any more exhaustive? I do not think so.
Who introduced a publishing policy which promoted Canadian interests and control in that vital cultural industry? We did. We, the Progressive Conservative Government of Canada, did. Who introduced a film policy which provides Canadian film production more money than ever before and which establishes Canada as a distinct market for foreign films for the first time in history? We did. We, the Progressive Conservative Government, did.
Who brought amendments to the Copyright Act so that authors and artists would begin to receive some fair treatment for their creative works? The Government led by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), that is who did it. Who is fighting it in the other place? The Liberal Senators. They do not want our artists and authors to receive fair compensation for their work. They are holding it up in the Senate.
As far as Canadian publishing and films are concerned, what did the Official Opposition say, bolstered by their socialist friends in the New Democratic Party? What did they do over 20 years in power? To use a much hackneyed expression, "the square root of nothing" is what they did over the last 20 years. Perhaps that is not quite accurate. They talked a lot about it, they attended cultural events and had their pictures taken with our great Canadian stars, but that is about it.

May 16, 1988
Supply
Nothing in the free trade agreement in any way, shape, or form prevents this Government, or any succeeding Government, from introducing other policies to protect and enhance Canada's cultural industries. As a Government we have already done so, and we will continue to do so.
In ending this part of my remarks, Madam Speaker, I might say it was difficult to explain to the American people our concern for protecting our cultural industries. It was difficult to get through to them. Because the culture in the United States has never been under attack or threatened, they could not comprehend why we in this country would worry so much about it. We did worry about it. We took the appropriate action, and we are very proud of what we accomplished.
As I understand it, the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood and her colleague, the Hon. Member for Essex- Windsor (Mr. Langdon), have a particular interest in the potential impact of the free trade agreement on the establishment of provincial auto insurance plans. The free trade agreement in no way prevents any provincial government from introducing such a plan. As I understand it, the Members are worried about Article 2010 which concerns the establishment of monopolies. It states as follows:
1. Subject to Article 2011, nothing in this Agreement shall prevent a Party from maintaining or designating a monopoly.
This is subject to the bilateral consultation provisions in the agreement.
First, if the Hon. Members are specifically referring to the Province of Ontario, and I am sure they both are because that is where the discussions have been going on at the present time on establishing a potential provincial auto insurance plan, we do not yet know the nature of that plan, or if the provincial Government has even decided to establish such a plan. But let us assume for the purposes of the argument that Ontario does so-perish the thought-but let us assume that it does. The plan could take several forms. For example, companies which currently sell auto insurance could end up being full participants in such a plan. If that is the case, and the United States firms have the same rights and obligations as Canadian firms under the plan, there would be no basis whatsoever under the free trade agreement for American complaints under the agreement.
Another possible arrangement could be the creation of a provincial auto insurance agency which would co-exist with private insurance companies. Again, the United States companies have the same rights and obligations as Canadian companies. The principle of national treatment is respected, and again there would be absolutely no basis for complaint.
What if the Government of Ontario established a provincial monopoly that excluded the private sector from the auto insurance business, if it just decided to take it over holus-bolus? First, under Article 2010 of the free trade agreement it would have every right to do so. Second, should the scheme give rise to expropriation, or nationalization of an investment,
the agreement provides for compensation at fair market value on a non-discriminatory basis.
In other words, if there is expropriation or nationalization, those that are being nationalized will receive fair compensation. Is that fair? Does that not make sense? In expropriation or nationalization, and the victims-and I use that term advisedly-would be compensated at fair market value. That is fairness.
The Hon. Member seems to be considering this issue from only one point of view. Apparently, she does not believe that Canadian firms are active in the United States and that they will enjoy exactly the same protection and benefits under the monopolies clause as U.S. firms will in Canada. Perhaps the Hon. Member does not care about the hundreds of Canadian firms that do business south of the border. Perhaps she thinks that Canadian firms do not invest, establish plants, or do much business in the United States market. The fact is that Canadians are major investors in the United States, and we have seen some of that lately. Our businesses have billions of dollars worth of investment there. If any state government decides one day that a state monopoly should be established in this, or in any other industry, Article 2010 will provide the Government of Canada and the Canadian businesses affected with a useful instrument for protecting Canadian interests there.
The Hon. Member and many of her colleagues keep making the same mistake about this country, about this Canada that we all love and are proud of. They underestimate what has taken place over the past 20 years or so. Their positions, proposals, and policies are consistently based on what Canada was in the late 1960s and not what Canada is today.
Why do the Members opposite not come to terms with the fact that the global economy has radically changed, and Canada has changed also. Why do they have this intellectual reflex to establish barriers instead of bridges to opportunities in the world economy? Why is it that labour thinkers and policy makers in countries such as Sweden and Great Britain are opting for policies to eliminate barriers to international trade and to stimulate market forces, whereas here in Canada the socialists, that great New Democratic Party, arm in arm with Shirley Carr and the Canadian Labour Congress, persist in opting for central planning models and technocratic intervention? I find it depressing, if not bizarre.
I have heard it in a couple of speeches today from both the Liberal Members and the New Democratic Party members that we are too small, we are not ready, we are too weak, we are vulnerable, or we are not able to adjust. Right down the line they underestimate Canadians. They think that they have all the knowledge and the ability over there, that they can control everything in this country. That is just not true.
With that type of pessimism and hopelessness, our forefathers would never have built this great country. The greatest moments of this country have been when it faced great challenges. Whether or not the Opposition chooses to see it, every day the 3 million Canadians' jobs that depend on trade
May 16, 1988

face great technological and competitive challenges in the global market-place. Those people are not saying that we cannot compete. They are not the ones who are opposing the trade agreement. They are saying that we can compete, and we will compete. But the Opposition persists in underestimating them. The opposition will continue to insist that big brother look over everybody's shoulder. Most Canadians have come to a very definite conclusion that, after bigger and bigger government, an enormous deficit, and mushrooming Crown corporations run by bureaucrats, big brother is a lousy manager. Canadians can see what has happened to the firms that were privatized by the Government.
For example, Firms like Canadair. Near my area, De Havilland employs 1,500 more people than when the Government had it, and it is going lickety-split. The Member from the riding where de Havilland is located fought that privatization. He said it will cost jobs. There are 1,500 more jobs. Fisheries Products International is now financially sound. It is employing more people than ever before. It is exciting. But, oh, no, the NDP do not think so. They think what is happening is terrible. They want those big deficits to come back. They want big brother back on the shoulders of Canadians. I wish they would wake up to the fact that big brother's time has come and gone. I will tell you whose time has come under this Government. It is the time of those Canadians who want to be free to build, to innovate, to trade and be rewarded for their initiative and enterprise as well as to provide assistance and protection to those Canadians who need it most.
I listened to the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) talk about the inadequate social services in the United States. I agree with her wholeheartedly. But she sets up a straw man and then proceeds to knock him down. We are not harmonizing our social programs, not one bit. As a matter of fact our social programs are the envy of the Americans. Why is a presidential candidate saying he would love to implement the health care program that we have in Canada? I have great faith in Canadians. I know Canadians believe that we do not want in any way, shape or form to destroy what we have built up in this country. Canadians know the last thing we want to do is to spoil the social safety net that has been developed. It is one of the things that makes us unique. I also know that if our economy is not doing well, if we are not trading, if we are not paying the bills and creating jobs, then we cannot pay for those wonderful social programs. That is the bottom line, Madam Speaker.
Canada has a great growth record going now, the best of the OECD countries, because we freed capable, innovative Canadians from the stifling and overbearing reach of the technocracy so favoured by the NDP and the Liberals. The free trade agreement is a vital part of that approach. It provides Canadians free and secure access to a market 10 times bigger than our own. This access will, in turn, put our businesses, large and small, in an even better position to
Supply
diversify the markets in Europe, in Japan and in all major markets of the world. I ask the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood, who brought this motion to the floor of the House today to consider what I have said and free herself from the ideological blinkers of her Party. I ask the Hon. Member to see Canada as a dynamic and growing part of the world, not as a timid northern territory lost in the shadow of its neighbour. Once she sees that and takes time to read the agreement and understand it, then I think we will have her support.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Parliamentary Secretary. Could he explain why the Government decided to include the service sector in this deal when it is the fastest growing sector in Canada and is creating the most jobs, particularly jobs for women? Can he explain why we are doing this when other countries have consistently resisted this through the GATT agreements? What are their reasons for not doing so? Why have we suddenly decided to open the doors to the Americans in the service sector?
I might point out, as the Hon. Member knows only too well, that the Macdonald Commission, when it did a very extensive and expensive study of our economy, came out in favour of free trade and did not include the service industry. Why is that? The Economic Council of Canada when it initially considered the impact of jobs did not consider the service sector. Does the Hon. Member not agree that the U.S. has a surplus of jobs in the service sector, so Americans are very anxious to export and infiltrate their service sector into other economies without any tariff barriers? Many Canadians feel that the Government has been naive in this area, the area where jobs will be most affected.
Why did the Government include our large and developing service sector in this deal, making us very vulnerable to the intrusion of the expanding American system when other countries refused to do so under GATT arrangements?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am glad the Hon. Member asked that question. First, the service industry accounts for two-thirds of the economy. It is the fastest growing industry in the world. Our GATT partners have asked for services to be part of the GATT negotiations in the Uruguay Round that is going on now. Services are very prominent on the agenda. To say our GATT partners have not wanted that is totally inaccurate.
Second, the Hon. Member for Hamilton East likes to give examples from her riding. I do too because that is what we know best. I have Picker X-ray in my riding which is a major company making huge X-rays for hospitals. It sells many into the United States, but it has trouble getting its service people down there to service equipment. After sales service, as the Hon. Member may or may not know, is a very important part of any contract. This is the maintenance and the upgrading of a particular product. We give Americans problems coming here to service equipment as they do with ours. Canadians and Americans with tool boxes under their arms were having to lie at the border, saying they were going on holidays. Things were

May 16, 1988

that bad. But the agreement will facilitate-it is not a labour agreement-a temporary movement for the servicing of products both ways.
Speak to our architects and see if they cannot compete in the United States. See if they do not feel that they can go there, do extremely well and bid on jobs in the U.S.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: They are elite Canadians, not ordinary Canadians.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade

speechtext: The Hon. Member is talking about ordinary Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: And women particularly in the service industry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
I have one architecture firm in my community which has three women architects and a number of support staff. The Hon. Member talks about ordinary Canadians. I have not met any more ordinary Canadians than those people. They are very fine people.
The service industry is now going through a revolution throughout the world. That is why some rules and regulations are being established to cover service. It only makes sense. The Hon. Member cannot ignore that end of it. I have a fellow in my constituency who is a brilliant individual when it comes to software programs. He has to lie every time he goes into the United States to sell his product. This agreement will facilitate that kind of movement. Canadians are good and we can go to the American market and sell. I have faith and pride in Canadians. The vice-president of IBM tells me that the most productive plant he has is in Bromont, Quebec.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: They said that about Firestone and closed it this year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade

speechtext:
Firestone was making a product that no one was buying. That was the problem.
The second most productive plant IBM has is in Don Mills, Ontario. The Hon. Member talks about moving firms back and forth. This will not happen. We in Canada are productive. I keep hearing about the southern United States. I keep asking my hon. friend why hasn't everybody moved down there now if it is so good? The tariffs are only 9.2 per cent average. People do not go because the southern U.S. does not have a well educated labour force and its force is not very productive. Our productivity is way higher than the southern States and in Florida where my hon. friend from Hamilton East likes to visit her in-laws. Hon. Members opposite put down Canadians every time they stand up and ask those questions.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: We are proud of unionized Canadians.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
