speechtext: The Hon. Member knocks Canadians. She doesn't think they are any good. She does not think they should go into the United States. We do. That is the difference between the socialists, the Liberals and the Conservatives.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Don't be so arrogant.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member brought up the issue of productivity. Does he really think that most American multinationals which are located in the States and 100 per cent American owned value productivity when push comes to shove, when they have to reorient, retract and shut down a plant? Firestone, which was located in my riding, was employing 1,400 people and had the most productive workforce of the Firestone chain of 13 plants across North America for three years running. It had won awards from the company for being the most productive, highly effective and economical plant. When the time came to find a plant to close down, why is it that the head office in Akron, Ohio, sent a three paragraph telex to the Hamilton plant saying that after over 100 years in that community, the plant is shut down?
If the Hon. Member thinks that an American multinational will make a dispassionate decision based specifically and solely on the bottom line, then he does not understand United States politics. Anyone sitting in a head office in Akron, Ohio, finds it much easier to close a plant in a foreign country than to close a plant in their own country. If productivity is the criterion, why was Firestone shut down in Hamilton?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because it was making a product that was not being purchased by the public, that was the problem. A lot of it has to do with the consumers. Goodyear closed in Hamilton but is opening up a new, modern plant and is hiring people in Canada.
I look at Oshawa. My friend, the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), does not mind foreign investment in his area.
Plants come and go. They have ever since they were established. In my community of Brampton, there were three or four industries that formed the base of Brampton. We were known as the flower town of Canada with Dale Estates and Calvert Estates there. There were 60 acres under glass producing beautiful roses, but they do not do that any more. It is just not economical to do that any more.
In Brampton, we had William's Shoe and Hewitson Shoe. Their plants became outmoded and their products were not accepted any longer. They closed. Those workers went on to new plants and new challenges. Change happens all the time. Over two million Canadians a year change their jobs. Change goes on all the time.
The Hon. Member wants to keep plants open, whether or not they have customers and whether or not they are productive. Just keep them, prop them up, give them more tax dollars, keep them going, shove them along. That is her attitude and it is also the socialist attitude, and it does not work.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to introduce my remarks, quite sincerely because these are things in which I believe and not just rhetoric, by
May 16, 1988

explaining why I, particularly as a New Democratic Member, oppose the Tory government trade deal. There are many reasons for this, of course, which I have no time to go into, but basically, we feel very strongly that this is not just a trade deal but it is much more. In fact, it changes the very nature of Canada.
As the social policy critic for my Party and as a person who is very concerned about health and welfare programs and status of women programs, I feel very strongly that the ethical and social principles for which we as Canadians stand and which most Canadians hold dear are really being threatened by this deal. These principles include our concern for each other which overrules market-place philosophy and the making of a buck, and particularly our concern for the poorer regions of Canada and our absolute conviction that we must help one another and therefore we need to have regional development programs. Another is our whole concept of social rights which I believe is imbedded in the Canadian psyche and certainly in Canadian institutions. I do not believe that that principle is embedded in the same way in the American society. We in Canada feel very strongly that we must have a floor of social programs so that when times get tough, people do not starve, although some who are on social assistance come pretty close to it.
We also believe that we must have a competitive economy and we have to be aware of market trends. However, we temper this belief with a certain amount of government planning, nationally, provincially and regionally. This combination of public and private which is very characteristic of Canada is another thing that makes us very strong. That is why we believe that we must have certain essential services that are public services. We also need to have certain Crown corporations which carry out functions that would not be carried out in the market-place if the Government were not involved to some degree.
These are things that are very important to us in Canada and these are things that the trade deal threatens. Many of us feel this very deeply. I do not think that my hon. friend has convinced me, and I doubt if he has convinced many concerned Canadians, through his remarks today that these things will not be affected.
Those of us in western Canada are rich in resources and have a resource-based economy, but we are subject to boom and bust cycles. Therefore, we must diversify. It has been very difficult to diversify. There are very fragile manufacturing and high-tech industries that are just getting started in British Columbia and these industries are threatened. They need government assistance to get started, and under this deal, they will not be able to get government assistance. We believe it will be very difficult for the Government to give leadership in helping western Canada to diversify.
The trade deal will also create in the future a continental energy policy. This concerns us greatly. Canada should have control over its own resources. We will not be able to charge
Supply
preferential prices for gas to secondary industries in Alberta such as the petrochemical industry, and I believe that has been done in the past.
We will have an open-door policy for U.S. investment under this deal and that will surely mean more branch plants than we already have and a transfer of jobs to the United States. It will certainly mean a move to do away with unions in Canada. Of course, that is a trend that this Government started, so it is not unreasonable at all that government Members are in favour of the trade deal.
Many of us do not agree that that is the way we want Canada to be. My friend, the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), has already spoken eloquently about the impact of the free trade deal on our culture and our sovereignty. We know that jobs will be lost in key industries and especially in industries that employ women. There will be less access to U.S. markets than the Government anticipates because the Americans were pretty cagey about what protections they wanted in the deal.
Some of the trade problems we face in British Columbia which are related to tariffs on shakes and shingles and the export taxes on softwood lumber will not be resolved by the free trade deal. The deal also makes us so absorbed with Canada-U.S. trade that we are completely disregarding in our thinking, our motivation and our policies the tremendous potential in the Pacific Rim.
I have just returned from Japan and Korea where I went with a parliamentary group led by the Hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees). The Governments and the business people in Japan and in Korea as well are very concerned that we are not giving them a fair deal because of our complete absorption with this trade deal.
I would like to speak particularly about the impact of the trade deal on women. Many of the remarks I will be making deal with facts that have been researched extensively by Marjorie Cohen, an outstanding economist who is very active in the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, a group which met this weekend.

Both NAC and our Party argue that the trade deal will have devastating consequences for Canadian working women. The deal opens Canada to free trade in services. The service sector contributes two-thirds of our national income and employs 70 per cent of our labour force. Some 83 per cent of service sector jobs are held by women. They will be jeopardized by a trade agreement in services. We are not talking about sophisticated, highly trained architects or highly skilled computer programmers. They will of course have some advantages. We are talking about the masses, particularly the 83 per cent of service sector jobs held by women. They will be jeopardized by this deal.

May 16, 1988
Supply
The deal will eliminate many clerical jobs in data processing by cancelling laws which now require data to be processed and stored in Canada. We have already, without a trade agreement, lost 180,000 data processing jobs. With the agreement that could go as high as 500,000.
In the manufacturing sector, industries most threatened by free trade are those that employ 66 per cent of women; textiles, clothing, food processing, electrical and electronic products, and leather products. There are a couple of industries in my riding where, given the threat of this deal and existing policies of the Government, women are losing jobs. Many of these women are immigrants whose English is not a strong asset. They work in the garment industry and the fish plant industry. Jobs are already being threatened and many more are likely to be threatened in the future. Many of them are immigrants, older women, or those with low levels of education, and they will be losing jobs. It is difficult for them to get into ESL language training programs, much less retraining for the high-tech jobs which the Parliamentary Secretary mentioned as one of the benefits of this deal.
The harmonizing pressures exerted by free trade will cause a drop in Canadian wages and working conditions. We know the Government and the trade deal will definitely undermine the trade union movement. Women will lose their unionized jobs, of which there are not enough anyway, and will be concentrated in low wage occupations. They will suffer the most.
The benefits and social programs which are the right of all Canadians will be threatened by the agreement. Child care and maternity benefits may be considered unfair subsidies by the U.S., which certainly does not give these programs a high priority. Women will be particularly hard hit by a loss of such benefits. Americans have weak health and safety regulations, lower wages, poorer environmental protection, and ineffective equal rights legislation. Our standards will be threatened and this will harm all Canadians.
I asked the Parliamentary Secretary why the Government included the service sector in this agreement. European countries have resisted this change and certainly Third World countries have been very concerned about it. The Macdonald Commission did not include the service industry in its study of trade. The Economic Council of Canada did not initially include it in its projections of the impact on jobs. Obviously this was added later. We know the Americans were very anxious to include this sector because they have a surplus of services and are only too eager to move their service industries into Canada with no tariff barriers and with a decline in the kind of unionized jobs we should be protecting in Canada.
This deal allows U.S. firms to move in and run institutions for a profit. They can even receive Canadian subsidies for institutions in the service field which they are already moving into Canada. U.S. firms are given the right to be treated as Canadian firms, whether they are located in the country or not. This kind of invasion will result in job losses, depressed
wages and working conditions for workers, particularly women.
Marjorie Cohen is an outstanding economist who specialized in this field and she said this deal will also severely affect the quality, accessibility and universality of our social services. I would like to refer people to the document she prepared called Americanizing Services. She made very many important points and I will be able to touch on only the highlights.
First, the trade deal talks about the management of all health and most social services. This includes management of hospitals, including general hospitals, mental hospitals, childrens' hospitals, management of other institutional services such as homes for the physically handicapped and disabled, homes for disturbed children, homes for single mothers, and the management of non-institutional services such as ambulances, rehab clinics and public service clinics. These services are up for grabs. Annex 1408 of the agreement, I think it is, will open these services to American firms coming into Canada, taking over and expanding the administration of these services. These are the areas of secondary health services which are not protected by the Canada Health Act. They are not protected by the five principles of medicare which are so important.
This deal makes it harder to protect these services from erosion. The federal Government left the door wide open for U.S chains to continue to own and operate homes for seniors, indeed chain day care operations which have been established for profit, not to serve children. They are already moving into Canada and this trade deal plus other government policies will certainly give considerable incentive to expand this program and we are very concerned about it.
Studies show that the standards are very minimal in these chain operations. Wages are very low and there is a high turnover of staff. There is not the same quality of service and there is no real protection in the sense that there is in nonprofit services. It is grossly unfair that such commercial operations, such low quality commercial operations will be eligible for Canadian subsidies. There is no protection against that happening.
A hospital can contract out its management. This is the trend in British Columbia already. The British Columbia Government is privatizing everything in the public service. It even wants to privatize the servicing of highways, and certainly all the human services. It is contracting out to non-union kinds of operators and when you add the trade deal to this along with federal government policies on privatization, it just creates a tremendous threat to the quality of our social service sector, particularly our health care services. We believe we should have much more in the way of public, non-profit systems. It has definitely been proven that this is better quality service. However, the trade deal will not encourage that.
The effect on the nursing care labour force will be very great. There will be a great increase in part-time jobs and computerized services to replace the human care that nurses
May 16, 1988

provide. Unionized jobs for nurses will also be threatened. This means poorer services for patients. There will be less time for personalized services in the hospitals and the same will be the case in for-profit day care services.
[DOT] (nio)
Another section which concerns us is Section 2010, the rules on monopolies. The new rules on monopolies will make it almost impossible for any government in Canada, and I think particularly of British Columbia of course, to extend public provision of services for those in the private sector. We are concerned about that because there are services which should be public services which, if we become the Government, we will not be able to return to the public sector.
Many of us have spoken about access to government services. Although the agreement does not explicitly say that service firms will not be given access to government subsidy, there is nothing in the agreement which allows the right to give preference to non-profit services in many cases where the Government provides a fee for service.
We are also concerned about the subsidy section. This is where people are saying there is likely to be a real threat to our social programs. The deal does not clarify the definition of a subsidy or what kinds of services and industries will be considered subsidized services in the future. As you know, the deal stipulates that during the next five to seven years negotiations will continue so that new rules about what constitutes a subsidy will be established.
This could include any of our social programs which are already considered subsidies by many Americans. Unemployment insurance, social service programs, old age pensions, and so on could very well be considered subsidies.
We have heard several Members speaking about women in jobs. I am not going to concentrate on that except to say that the service sector concerns women, who are still the poorest sector of our society, who will be the biggest losers if we allow the erosion of social programs and the part-time jobs which will result from privatization. This trade deal is a great threat to women's jobs in particular.
Finally, the Parliamentary Secretary wants to debate child care programs at another time. We will not debate it at another time. The national strategy on child care is the forerunner of what we will see developing with this trade deal. It leaves the door wide open. In fact, it encourages provinces to develop and fund for-profit child care services. So it is there already and there is nothing in this deal which will protect for-profit child care. As was pointed out by one of the previous speakers, child care in the United States is of very poor quality. They do not even have maternity and parental leave policies there.
That is because the United States views social services from a market-place point of view. Making profits rather than service to people is their goal. We do not want this in Canada.
Supply
We want services, particularly child care services, that are concerned with children, pay decent wages to care givers, and will have public subsidies for good quality child care.
I could go on and on, Madam Speaker, but I see that my time is up. In conclusion, we are very concerned about this trade deal as are growing numbers of Canadians, the more they study and learn about this deal. It is basically a sell-out of Canada. I say that with great emphasis. It is particularly harmful to Canadian women. We will do everything in our power to stop this deal and to enable the people to express their views in an election.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Member is from western Canada. In her province two of the three major industries are forestry products and mining.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: What about fishing?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Of course fishing is another one. Does the Member not think that it is in the interests of a great many British Columbians to have a more secure access to the United States market than they have had during the past year in terms of shakes and shingles, softwood lumber, and fish? There is a long list of items in western Canada that have been harassed by U.S. trade laws and actions under those trade laws.
Has the Member looked, for example, at the recent data of the Canada West Foundation which shows that large numbers of western Canadian jobs would be more secure if this trade agreement goes ahead than they are at present? At present what you might call anarchy exists in our trading relations with that market.
The Member might wish to do more trade with Japan and other countries of Asia and the Pacific, China included, of course. The reality, as she probably knows, is that approaching two-thirds of the exported goods and services from western Canada go to the United States whether or not she or I like it. In other words, by my figures the pay cheques of roughly 600,000 western Canadians depend on access to that market.
With regard to the social programs and the seven years, at least she is more responsible than the Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) who said unequivocally that all our social programs will go down the drain if we form this agreement. This Member, if I remember correctly, said that they could be changed by the seven years of negotiation. Does the Member not think that it is important to the livelihoods of young people, middle-aged people, and the next generation to have some security of access to the United States?
Bob White is eviscerally opposed to this agreement even though, as I said this morning, we have had, for all intents and purposes, free trade in the auto sector since 1968 except for a few months in 1980 and 1981. The Member's Party calls it managed trade but it has, in fact, worked as free trade since 1968, three years after the Auto Pact.

May 16, 1988
Supply
Does the Member have to take Bob White's word on this issue when she and I know that western Canada needs this agreement? All provincial governments in western Canada and all independent bodies of research except for Mr. Bob White, as far as I can see, know that this agreement is in the interests of men and women throughout Canada. Does the Member not think that the prospect of having a job and a pay cheque at the end of the month is a fairly important social program to Canadians throughout the country?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I agree completely that having a job with a decent pay cheque is extremely important. It should be a basic right of all Canadians. This is particularly important to Canadian women. The point of what I was saying is that Canadian women, who are already marginalized and earn 60 cent dollars compared to men, will be really hurt by this deal. I made that point in my remarks with great sincerity.
The Hon. Member asked many questions and made many comments in his statement. As far as the western provinces are concerned, I am surprised that he seems so naive about it. I visited his Province of Alberta a few months ago and found considerable anxiety there. If any part of Canada needs to diversify, it is the West. We want secondary industries and more opportunities for secondary manufacturing jobs. We want to be able to export to places other than the United States. It is this open door policy which is a real giveaway to the United States which concerns us so much.
As far as the problems which we have had in British Columbia in the forest industry and the fisheries, as far as I can understand there is nothing in this deal to solve those problems. In fact, they are still there. I know that the Member of our Party who will speak next will comment on this further. I have a very close relationship with fishing people in my riding, particularly women working in the fish plants, and they are very concerned that this deal will not solve any of the problems they are facing. IWA members are solidly against this and the forest industry has real reservations in many instances.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I very much appreciated the discussion by my hon. colleague from Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) about the situation of women and the effect of the trade deal on their job opportunities in particular. I would like to ask her a question about the political aspects of the deal. She is a western Member and I am a former British Columbian.
It is my experience that westerners are patriotic Canadians who are proud of their Canadian institutions. They want an independent Canada and take pride in our public social programs. They take pride in our cultural institutions which are nationally funded and which we have operated differently from the Americans. Westerners are no less patriotic than any other Canadian. They may have their gripes against the East on some issues, but they are true Canadians and want strong
Canadian institutions. They pay their taxes and want that money to go into regional diversification, social programs, old age pensions, medicare and all of those programs, the same as Canadians from coast to coast.
Will my colleague comment on the loss of political sovereignty and the weakening of the powers of the federal and provincial governments to create and expand social and cultural programs for the good of the people within their territories?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not think I have to say that westerners believe in Canada. Of course we believe in Canada and are very proud Canadians. Sometimes we think central Canada should listen a little more. The Parliamentary Secretary made some very central Canadian comments earlier and said nothing about some concerns of the West. However, there is no question that we feel very strongly about Canada. We believe strongly in the potential of the Pacific Rim and that our trade relationship in this area is not being adequately developed.
As far as social programs in British Columbia are concerned, I am deeply ashamed of our Premier for what he is trying to do to undermine social programs and social service jobs in that province. This deal will add to that threat, and that is one reason why an increasing number of British Columbians are joining anti-free trade lobbies and coalitions. British Columbians are real fighters, as they are on the Prairies.
We are very proud that British Columbia is a highly unionized province. The Tories constantly talk about Bob White and Shirley Carr. Not only are they paranoid, they should have a guilt complex because they are trying to destroy unions in this country. Their policy of privatization and this free trade deal will certainly contribute to that. There is nothing they would like better than to eliminate unionized jobs for contracting out, to put women in part time jobs so they can return to the home and so on. I am very much afraid that rather than look to the future of Canada, this policy will take us back.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I listen, I understand the dichotomy to which Canada would be reduced if we had a war of wills between those on the extreme right and those on the extreme left. This is not a debate between General Motors and Bob White. This is a debate on a free trade deal that affects every Canadian, including those who are not necessarily tied to General Motors or the Canadian Autoworkers Union. It concerns people who are in business and members of unions and see for themselves and their families great changes and potentially great harm.
How does the Hon. Member respond to the Government's claim that the trade deal will be a cure-all for the problem of regional disparity in this country? Presumably, the various states in the United States are the beneficiaries of free trade within those United States, but there is still regional disparity
May 16, 1988

in many of the southern states. That regional disparity is growing in some of the rust belt, or northeast United States.
The Government would tell a province like Newfoundland or an area like Cape Breton or parts of northern Canada that this free trade deal will solve their regional disparity, yet the reality in the United States is that gross regional disparity exists notwithstanding the fact they have all the so-called advantages of the American economy. How does the Hon. Member respond to that?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, perhaps my hon. friend was not in the House when I began my remarks. I stated clearly that what concerns me and many Canadians is that Canada is unique because we care about each other in the different regions of Canada. We have a system in which there are certain written and unwritten social rights, including a concern for all regions so that people have equal opportunity and equal protection in all regions.
We must have regional development programs and the Hon. Member is absolutely right that this trade deal will gradually erode them. While the Government says this will not happen, the five to seven years in which to define subsidies is certainly a cause for concern.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was rather hoping today that we might have a debate based upon the free trade agreement. However, what we have had is another debate with a lot of rhetoric, exposing once again what I call the myths of free trade.
I want to examine some of those myths this afternoon because I think it is important to set the record straight on what is and is not in this particular trade agreement. Since it was just mentioned, let me deal with myth No. 1. It is that regional development programs are at risk. We have heard that over and over this afternoon. I do not know how to respond to that, except to say that it is pretty close to absolute nonsense. They are no more at risk under the free trade agreement than they are now.
Under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, which has been mentioned so often in this debate, Government subsidies are recognized as legitimate tools of governments to help promote regional development. All that GATT requires is that countries should not use subsidies in a way that injures other countries. Subsidies in themselves are not illegal.
Under existing Canada and U.S. law as well, subsidies are only countervailable by the importing nations if they are not generally available. Those persons who would have us believe that regional development programs would go down the drain should know that the ones they are talking about are generally available.
Only very few of the Canadian regional development subsidies have been challenged as countervailable in the United States. Only a fraction of those that have been
Supply
challenged were found by U.S. authorities to be injurious to American producers. Since 1980, no countervailing duty on a regional development Subsidy has exceeded 1 per cent of the export price. One of the advantages of being an engineer is that I always ask myself, what are the numbers? Never mind the rhetoric, what are the numbers? I remind people of the 1 per cent of the export price. Even if the subsidies were found to do harm, we can still put them on if we wish. It is entirely our decision. The free trade agreement does not in any way take away that decision from us.
Let me go now to what I call myth No. 2. I have so many myths here that I am going to lose count. The next myth is that Canada's cultural sovereignty is at stake. How? Article 2005 of the agreement stipulates that with four very limited exceptions, nothing in the agreement impedes Canada's ability to pursue cultural policies and programs of its own. If we look at the four that are taken out, we find they are hardly going to shake this country's cultural policy. We are going to eliminate tariffs on musical instruments, cassettes, films and records. In other words, the U.S. will be able to export records and tapes into Canada free of tariffs. We will be able to do the same.
Under Article 2006, both Canada and the United States will provide copyright protection to owners of television programs broadcast by distant stations and retransmitted by cable companies. Article 2007 is the typeset and printing section. None of these changes our ability as a nation to do what we have always done, to call for Canadian content regulations, to support the CBC, to support our national galleries, to support the Canada Council, and to support our artists and writers. None of these things are changed in this agreement. There is a myth out there that we have given up our cultural sovereignty. In fact, culture has been taken right out of it. There is nothing in the agreement that we do now that we cannot do.
The next myth is that free trade will destroy Canada's social programs. Well, we have heard this afternoon about how somehow or other-no one says quite how-we are going to harmonize our health care system. Why would we want to harmonize anything that is working very well right now? There is nothing in this agreement that talks about harmonizing our health care system. It is our system. It will remain our system.
My opposition colleagues talked often about the GATT today but under GATT, generally available social programs are not countervailable. Why should we be concerned about changing our health care system? It is another straw man put up to frighten people. As an aside, you know, Madam Speaker, and 1 know, that the United States has already examined the fishermen's disputed unemployment insurance benefits, and they were found not countervailable.
Finally, on this one subject, the preamble of the agreement itself clearly sets out Canada's ability to take measures to defend the public welfare. We are no less Canadian because we are entering into a free trade agreement with the United States. In fact, it is so typically Canadian that we would reach

May 16, 1988
Supply
out to have more trade. That is what Canada is all about. Our health care system is in no way in danger, neither are our social programs. Read the agreement, Madam Speaker, that is where it says they are not at risk. They have been taken out of the agreement.
Another myth, and the committee heard this myth when it was on the road travelling across the country, startling as it may seem and almost incomprehensible to Members of this Chamber, is that free trade will lead to a flood of American pornography and hand-guns coming into this country. One person even said that the streets of Toronto will not be safe. I do not know how something like this gets started, but it has about as much relevance to the free trade debate as the price of hot dogs at Maple Leaf Stadium. Pornography is already dealt with under the authority of Canada's Criminal Code. There is nothing in the agreement that says we have to change Canada's Criminal Code. That is nonsense. The GATT already provides the authority for Canada to control the import of both pornography and firearms. Article 407, chapter 5 and chapter 12 of the free trade agreement makes it clear that these powers remain absolutely untouched.
The next myth is that free trade will unleash wide-open competition in services. Article 1402 of the agreement makes it clear that existing laws and regulations governing services remain untouched. The agreement relates only to future laws and regulations. I am always concerned when people talk about services as if somehow or other this is a departure that will ruin Canada. But I ask, when the GATT was established in 1947, what was the world trading in? It was trading primarily in goods. In 1987, if we were establishing the GATT, it is incomprehensible to me that it would not talk about goods and services because services have become more important in the world in terms of trade than goods. In some instances, I do not know how one tells the difference between what are goods and what is a service. What is a floppy disk? Is it a goods or is it a service? Of course, it is a combination of both. To say that service should not be in a modern trading agreement, to me, hearkens back to the horse and buggy days. Of course, they belong in a trade agreement. Canadians are good at these sorts of things. We have nothing to fear in terms of services. We sell our services across the whole world and we want this agreement to be the forerunner of what the GATT should be. We will win on this at the GATT.
Another myth is that Canada's trucking industry will be destroyed. The services annex of the agreement does not include transportation, not at all. Like the cultural and social programs, the trucking industry is not affected in any way by the agreement. "Canada should depend on multilateral negotiations in the GATT rather than bilateral free trade with the United States". We have heard that statement several times through the course of the last few months. Well, of course, Canada depends on both, and will continue to do so.
The free trade agreement itself sets out our continuing commitment to ensure that we trade multilaterally in all aspects. The agreement that we have here is consistent in every way with Article XXIV of the GATT, the article that provides the framework for negotiating the free trade agreement.
Both countries retain their existing GATT rights and obligations. It strikes me that not many of the people who are concerned about this and talk only of the GATT are traders. Not many traders would tell one to stick only to the GATT. Most of the talkers do but not many traders do. If one is a trader then one knows that it is easiest in Canada to trade with the United States. It is our natural market. That is what Canadian business does. It moves with the United States.
There have been two Governments in the last few years that have tried to switch that around. Mr. Diefenbaker's Government tried to do it, as did Mr. Trudeau's Government, with a spectacular lack of success. Those things cannot be dictated to traders and to business people. They must be allowed to do their own thing. They would prefer to trade with the United States.
We can therefore use this agreement and our experience in trading with the Americans, our ability to compete with them and our ability to produce world product mandates, to then trade with the rest of the world, which is what part of this is all about. Both the United States and Canada are founding members of the GATT. We want the GATT to be successful, but we want the GATT to move away from where it is now.
Let me finish by talking for just a moment about child care, something which we have heard so much about this afternoon. There is nothing in the agreement that foresees or encourages, provides for or allows health and social services to become tradable services. If a United States firm comes into Canada to operate a child care facility it may do so. However, if we read the agreement, we find that it is not entitled to national treatment for the conduct and operation of that facility since that right flows only to covered services. Day care is not covered.
Let us do away with the myth and let us look at the agreement. There is nothing in this agreement that causes a change in any Canadian standard or criterion governing services within the health, education, social service or child care field.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POLITICAL SOVEREIGNTY

Hon. Members now want to talk about health management. That is a good one for Canada since, once again, people do not understand what Canada is doing. They are so afraid of the United States that they do not understand.
Do Hon. Members know who will win with respect to health care facility management? It will be Canadians going down to the U.S. marketing and operating their facilities. We do it now. We are big operators there, and we will continue to be

big operators. Most of the people who talk about this have no experience in running a health care facility, none whatsoever. Some of us have. Some of us know how good we are.
One of the tragedies about this is that so few people have yet to learn that this agreement is typically Canadian. It is an agreement that reaches out and says: "We are good. We can do it. Let us have the opportunity".
